Filed 10/21/26 Tyron Street Acquisition Trust v. Moshe CA2/4 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 
California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on 
opinions not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(a). This 
opinion has not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115(a). 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 
DIVISION FOUR 

TYRON STREET ACQUISITION 
TRUST I, A DELAWARE 
STATUTORY TRUST, 
 Plaintiff and Respondent, 
 v. 
YAIR BEN MOSHE, 
 Defendant and Appellant. 
B351583 
(Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. 
24STCV10832) 

APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of Los 
Angeles County, Gary D. Roberts, Judge. Affirmed. 
Law Offices of Jacob Reich, Jacob Reich for Defendant and 
Appellant. 
Donahue Fitzgerald, Mark D. Epstein and Garrett Burton; 
Snell & Wilmer, Andrew B. Still and Eric S. Pezold for Plaintiff 
and Respondent. 

2 

This appeal arises from cross-motions for summary 
judgment regarding lien priority over two adjacent parcels of real 
property. Tyron Street Acquisition Trust I (Tyron) contends it is 
entitled to lien priority under the doctrine of equitable 
subrogation. Yair Ben Moshe counters that equitable 
subrogation does not apply because it would elevate Tyron’s deed 
of trust to a superior position and would directly prejudice 
Moshe’s deed of trust. The trial court granted Tyron’s motion 
and denied Moshe’s, concluding that equitable subrogation 
applies in this case as a matter of law. We affirm. 
BACKGROUND 
I. Facts 
A. The Properties and the 1968 Covenant 
This case concerns lien priority over two adjacent parcels of 
real property commonly known as 1303 and 1305 Laveta Terrace 
in Los Angeles (the property). On May 29, 1968, a covenant was 
recorded against the property (the 1968 covenant). The 1968 
covenant provides that the two lots “shall be held as one parcel 
and no portion shall be sold separately.” On December 3, 2014, 
Reposition Laveta, LLC (Reposition) acquired title to both lots by 
a single grant deed. Thereafter, Reposition borrowed money 
against the property as detailed below. 
B. The Easy Financial Deeds of Trust 
On June 10, 2021, two separate deeds of trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC (Easy Financial) were recorded in the Los 
Angeles County’s Recorder’s Office, each encumbering one of the 

3 

two adjacent properties.1 One deed of trust secured a loan of 
$1,725,000 and encumbered the property known as 1305 Laveta 
Terrace. The other deed of trust secured a loan of $862,500 and 
encumbered the adjacent property commonly known as 1303 
Laveta Terrace. 
C. Moshe’s Deed of Trust 
On September 30, 2022, Moshe made an $800,000 loan to 
Reposition, secured by a deed of trust which encumbered both 
Laveta Terrace properties. 
D. The Churchill Loan and Payoff of the Easy 
Financial Loans 
On or about March 2, 2023, Churchill Funding LLC 
(Churchill) made a loan to Reposition in the amount of 
$2,793,750.00, secured by a deed of trust recorded on March 7, 
2023. The single deed of trust encumbered both Laveta Terrace 
properties. 
As an express condition of funding, Churchill required that 
its deed of trust record in first position and that all senior liens 
be cleared or paid through escrow. It specifically conditioned 
funding on issuance of a lender’s title policy insuring first 
priority. The preliminary report of title that Churchill received 
from Stewart Title Guaranty Company (Stewart Title) while 
underwriting the loan disclosed the Easy Financial deeds of trust, 

1 Tyron claims that on October 10, 2019, before the Easy 
Financial deeds of trust were recorded, a deed of trust in favor of 
Maxim Commercial Capital, securing a loan of $1,800,000, was 
recorded. Moshe asserts the record does not establish that the Maxim 
deed of trust remained an outstanding encumbrance when Moshe 
recorded his deed of trust. But as Moshe concedes, we need not decide 
this dispute because it has no bearing on the dispositive issues on 
appeal. 

4 

but did not disclose Moshe’s deed of trust. The lender’s title 
policy issued by Stewart Title also did not disclose Moshe’s deed 
of trust and insured Churchill’s deed of trust as first priority. 
Following the payoffs of the Easy Financial loans—
$1,777,635.28 for the first Easy Financial loan and $903,059.16 
for the second Easy Financial loan—both Easy Financial deeds of 
trust were reconveyed and released from the property of record. 
On January 26, 2024, Churchill assigned its deed of trust to 
Tyron by recorded Assignment of Security Instruments. The 
assignment included the same legal description applicable to the 
two Laveta Terrace properties. 
II. Procedural Background and the Trial Court’s 
Rulings 
On April 30, 2024, Tyron filed a complaint against Moshe 
for (1) equitable subrogation, (2) injunctive relief, (3) quiet title to 
a mortgage lien, and (4) declaratory relief. Tyron alleged that the 
purpose of the Churchill loan was to refinance and pay off the full 
balances the borrower owed on pre-existing mortgage loans that 
encumbered the property and that “both the Borrower and 
Churchill Funding, and by extension Tyron Street as the assignee 
and successor-in-interest to Churchill Funding, intended for, and 
expected that the full balance of the Loan funds would be used to 
pay off and retire the Borrower’s pre-existing secured debt on the 
Property in its entirety, and that the new Tyron Street Deed of 
Trust that secured the Loan would constitute a first priority 
position lien on the Property.” 
Tyron moved for summary adjudication of its first, third, 
and fourth causes of action. It argued that the undisputed 
evidence demonstrated the Churchill loan funds were used to 
satisfy senior encumbrances and that Churchill and Tyron 

5 

reasonably believed the loan was secured in first position. Thus, 
according to Tyron, its deed of trust—recorded after Moshe’s—
has priority under the doctrine of equitable subrogation. In 
support of its motion, Tyron submitted the declaration of 
Matthew Dameron, Director of Asset Management for Churchill 
Funding I, LLC (the master servicer and attorney-in-fact for 
Tyron), which attached the loan file records and the escrow 
disbursements paying off the Easy Financial loans. 
Moshe opposed the motion and filed evidentiary objections 
to Dameron’s declaration. Moshe argued Tyron is not entitled to 
summary adjudication because the Easy Financial loans were 
void or defective, equitable subrogation is not applicable because 
it would prejudice Moshe, there is no admissible evidence 
supporting the essential elements of equitable subrogation, and 
material issues of fact exist regarding whether Churchill had 
knowledge of Moshe’s deed of trust. 
Moshe also filed his own motion for summary judgment or, 
in the alternative, for summary adjudication on the ground that 
equitable subrogation does not apply as a matter of law because, 
according to Moshe, “granting subrogation will not just put 
[Tyron] in the shoes in which the preexisting lien holder was, 
rather it will elevate [Tyron] giving him a position far superior to 
that previously held by the prior lien holder whose debt was paid 
off and it will put [Moshe] in a position, substantially inferior to 
the position he would have been in, had the preexisting loans not 
been replaced by the Churchill Loan.” 
After a hearing, the trial court issued a 21-page written 
ruling granting Tyron’s motion and denying Moshe’s motion. The 
court concluded no material issues of fact exist as to whether 
equitable subrogation is applicable. Thus, the court granted 

6 

summary adjudication of Tyron’s claim for equitable subrogation, 
as well as Tyron’s derivative claims for quiet title and declaratory 
relief. 
The clerk then entered dismissal, at Tyron’s request, of the 
only remaining claim for injunctive relief. The trial court entered 
judgment establishing two equitable liens in favor of Tyron as 
follows: (1) Tyron’s “Deed of Trust is equitably subrogated to the 
priority position against 1305 Laveta Terrace, Los Angeles, 
California 90026 that was held by the Deed of Trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC recorded . . . on June 10, 2021 . . . for the 
principal amount of $1,777,635.28 plus accrued interest thereon” 
and (2) Tyron’s “Deed of Trust is equitably subrogated to the lien 
priority position against 1303 Laveta Terrace, Los Angeles, 
California 90026 that was held by the Deed of Trust in favor of 
Easy Financial LLC recorded . . . on June 10, 2021 . . . for the 
principal amount of $903,059.16 plus accrued interest thereon.” 
Moshe timely appealed. 
DISCUSSION 
I. Standard of Review 
A party is entitled to summary judgment only if there is no 
triable issue of material fact and the party is entitled to judgment 
as a matter of law. (Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (c).) A triable 
issue of fact exists if the evidence would allow a reasonable trier 
of fact to find the fact in favor of the party opposing summary 
judgment. (Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co. (2001) 25 Cal.4th 
826, 850.) 
We review the trial court’s ruling on a summary judgment 
motion de novo, liberally construe the evidence in favor of the 
party opposing the motion, and resolve all doubts concerning the 
evidence in favor of the opponent. (Miller v. Department of 

7 

Corrections (2005) 36 Cal.4th 446, 460.) “We must affirm a 
summary judgment if it is correct on any of the grounds asserted 
in the trial court, regardless of the trial court’s stated reasons.” 
(Grebing v. 24 Hour Fitness USA, Inc. (2015) 234 Cal.App.4th 
631, 636—637.) 
We generally review a trial court’s ruling on evidentiary 
objections for an abuse of discretion. As to evidentiary rulings 
made in connection with a motion for summary judgment, 
however, there is a split of authority. Some courts have held 
such evidentiary rulings are reviewed for abuse of discretion 
(Martin v. Trustees of California State University (2023) 97 
Cal.App.5th 149, 161; Butte Fire Cases (2018) 24 Cal.App.5th 
1150, 1169), while other courts have held that some or all written 
objections should be reviewed de novo (Pipitone v. Williams 
(2016) 244 Cal.App.4th 1437, 1450—1451; Strobel v. Johnson & 
Johnson (2021) 70 Cal.App.5th 796, 816—817.) “We will follow 
the weight of authority and apply the abuse of discretion 
standard.” (Schmidt v. Citibank, N.A. (2018) 28 Cal.App.5th 
1109, 1118.) 
II. The Trial Court Did Not Err by Applying the 
Doctrine of Equitable Subrogation 
California law generally follows the “first in time, first in 
right” system of lien priorities. (See Civ. Code, § 2897 [“Other 
things being equal, different liens upon the same property have 
priority according to the time of their creation”].) However, the 
“doctrine of equitable subrogation is an exception to the first in 
time, first in right rule and applies in those situations where 
equity requires a different result.” (JP Morgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
v. Banc of America Practice Solutions, Inc. (2012) 209 
Cal.App.4th 855, 860 (Chase).) 

8 

Nearly a century ago, our Supreme Court stated the 
general rule applicable to a lender’s entitlement to equitable 
subrogation: “ ‘One who advances money to pay off an 
encumbrance on realty at the instance of either the owner of the 
property or the holder of the incumbrance, either on the express 
understanding, or under circumstances from which an 
understanding will be implied, that the advance made is to be 
secured by a first lien on the property, is not a mere volunteer; 
and in the event the new security is for any reason not a first lien 
on the property, the holder of such security, if not chargeable 
with culpable and inexcusable neglect, will be subrogated to the 
rights of the prior encumbrancer under the security held by him, 
unless the superior or equal equi

leads.caseName: Dworman v. PHH Mortgage Services
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
leads.text:
United States Court of Appeals 
For the First Circuit 

No. 25-1407 
ALAN DWORMAN, 
Plaintiff, Appellant, 
v. 
PHH MORTGAGE SERVICES; OCWEN LOAN SERVICING, LLC, 

Defendants, Appellees, 
FIRST OHIO BANC & LENDING, INC., 

Defendant. 

APPEAL FROM THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT 
FOR THE DISTRICT OF MASSACHUSETTS 

[Hon. Margaret R. Guzman, U.S. District Judge] 

Before 

Barron, Chief Judge, 
Gelpí and Aframe, Circuit Judges. 

 J. Mark Dickison , with whom Brendan P. Slean and Lawson & 
Weitzen, LLP were on brief, for appellant. 

 Marissa I. Delinks, with whom Maura K. McKelvey and Hinshaw 
& Culbertson LLP were on brief, for appellees. 

October 21, 2026 

- 2 - 
AFRAME, Circuit Judge . After defaulting on a home 
mortgage loan, Alan Dworman agreed with his loan servicer that if 
he met certain repayment conditions, a portion of his loan balance 
would be forgiven. Dworman failed to meet those conditions. He 
nonetheless claimed that the loan servicer and its successor had 
forgiven his debt by issuing him an Internal Revenue Service 
("IRS") Form 1099-C, entitled "Cancellation of Debt," and through 
certain other conduct related to the debt's collection . They 
disagreed. 
With his debt unforgiven, Dworman sued his loan servicer 
and its successor in state court, asserting claims for breach of 
contract, breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing, 
and violation of the Massachusetts consumer protection statute , 
Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A ("Chapter 93A") , as well as seeking 
declaratory relief . Based on diversity jurisdiction, the 
defendants removed the case to federal court. In due course, the 
defendants moved for summary judgment on all claims. The district 
court rejected Dworman's contention that it would be premature to 
rule on the summary judgment motion without permitting additional 
discovery and then granted the motion. Dworman appeals from the 
denial of his request for additional discovery and the grant of 
summary judgment. We affirm in both respects. 
- 3 - 
I. 
A. 
In 2007, Dworman obtained a $549,600 mortgage loan from 
First Ohio Banc & Lending, Inc. ("First Ohio Banc") to refinance 
an existing mortgage on his Massachusetts residence. The following 
year, Dworman lost his job and fell behind on paying his mortgage. 
In early 2016, Dworman sought mortgage assistance from Ocwen Loan 
Servicing, LLC ("Ocwen"), his loan servicer at the time. Ocwen 
offered Dworman a "Home Affordable Loan Modification Trial Period 
Plan," which Dworman accepted in July 2016. Under the plan, after 
successfully making three reduced monthly payments, Dworman became 
eligible for a permanent loan modification agreement. In November 
2016, Dworman entered into such an agreement with Ocwen (the "2016 
Agreement"). The U.S. Department of Treasury paid Ocwen a $1,200 
incentive for implementing the 2016 Agreement. 
Per the 2016 A greement, Dworman's delinquent taxes, 
insurance, and interest were capitalized into a new principal 
balance of $821,864.94. Section 3(c) of the 2016 Agreement 
provided that $465,114.94 of this balance would be deferred (the 
"Deferred Principal Balance") and that Dworman would not pay 
interest or make monthly payments on the Deferred Principal Balance 
until the loan's maturity date. It further stated that $406,714.94 
of the Deferred Principal Balance (the "Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount") was "eligible for forgiveness." So long as 
- 4 - 
Dworman was "not in default on [his] new payments such that the 
equivalent of three full monthly payments are due and unpaid on 
the last day of any month," one third of the Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount would be forgiven on each of the first, second, 
and third anniversaries of September 1, 2016. 
On December 5, 2016, four days after the 2016 Agreement 
became effective, Ocwen sent Dworman an IRS Form 1099-C, entitled 
"Cancellation of Debt," which listed $406,714.94 as the "[a]mount 
of debt discharged." The Form 1099-C notifies the IRS of the 
discharged amount because it may be considered income for federal 
tax purposes. Dworman filed the Form 1099 -C with his 2016 tax 
return, reporting the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount as 
income. 
Dworman missed his first modified mortgage payment and 
continued to fall behind on payments. Throughout 2017, Ocwen sent 
Dworman numerous communications indicating his arrearages. And in 
May of that year, Ocwen assisted Dworman in trying to bring his 
account current by sending him a temporary repayment agreement. 
Dworman's default status continued into 2018, and Ocwen 
issued further delinquency notices. In mid -March 2018, for 
example, Ocwen sent Dworman a notice advising that his loan had 
been referred to counsel to begin foreclosure proceedings and 
included a notice of debt indicating that "[t]he amount of debt as 
of March 12, 2018 is $832,109.93." Later that month, Dworman 
- 5 - 
entered into a repayment agreement with Ocwen, but he nonetheless 
remained delinquent. In September 2018, Ocwen sent a mortgage 
statement reflecting that the loan was 169 days delinquent and 
that Dworman's total principal balance was $813,995.09, comprising 
a regular principal balance of $348,880.15 and a Deferred Principal 
Balance of $465,114.94. Ocwen sent Dworman similar mortgage 
statements in February and April 2019; each noted Dworman's 
delinquency and listed the Deferred Principal Balance as 
$465,114.94. 
On June 4, 2019, PHH Mortgage Corporation ("PHH") sent 
Dworman a notice informing him that it had merged with Ocwen and 
that PHH was now servicing his loan (the "June 2019 Transfer 
Notice"). Dworman acknowledge d receiving this Notice, which 
included an addendum indicating that the principal balance for 
Dworman's account as of June 1, 2019, was $342,838.62. The June 
2019 Transfer Notice did not , however, mention the Deferred 
Principal Balance. On August 13, 2019, PHH sent Dworman a letter 
amending the Notice, stating that it had omitted the Deferred 
Principal Balance and clarifying that "[t]he correct principal 
balance as of [June 1, 2019] which includes the deferred principal 
balance was: $807,953.56. " Dworman denies having received this 
letter, although it was sent to the same address as the June 2019 
Transfer Notice. 
- 6 - 
On April 6, 2020, in response to Dworman's request for 
a payoff letter on his loan, PHH notified Dworman that the Deferred 
Principal Balance "was not forgiven," as Dworman had been 
delinquent in his loan payments on the first anniversary of the 
2016 Agreement. Dworman admit ted that he received this 
notification. In 2020, Dworman caught up on his loan obligations 
and has since made timely payments. 
Dworman filed suit in January 2023, naming First Ohio 
Banc, Ocwen, and PHH as defendants.1 The parties then engaged in 
discovery, during which Dworman directed document requests to 
Ocwen. Relevant here, Dworman sought documents from Ocwen 
"relating to any tax write offs, financial benefits and incentives 
extended to Ocwen . . . including but not limited to Ocwen's tax 
filings 2016 to present." In Dworman's vie w, these documents 
pertained to whether Ocwen had received the benefit of a tax 
write-off for issuing the Form 1099-C, which would tend to suggest 
that it treated the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount as 
discharged. By that time, the mortgagee and note holder had moved 
from First Ohio Banc to Deutsche Bank National Trust Company as 
Trustee for IndyMac INDX Mortgage Loan Trust 2007 -AR17, Mortgage 
Pass-Through Certificates Series 2007 -AR17 ( "Deutsche Bank 
Trust"). Deutsche Bank Trust was not named in these requests, nor 

1 Following the appeal, Dworman voluntarily dismissed his 
claims against First Ohio Banc, the original mortgagee. 
- 7 - 
was it ever named a party to Dworman's suit. Ocwen objected to 
Dworman's request for its tax filings on relevance grounds and did 
not produce them during the litigation. 
B. 
Following discovery, Ocwen and PHH (collectively, "the 
defendants") moved for summary judgment on all claims. Dworman 
opposed the motion, both on the merits and because it was premature 
insofar as he needed further discovery into Ocwen's 2016 tax 
filings.2 On the latter argument, the district court determined 
that Ocwen's refusal to produce its 2016 tax filings posed no 
impediment to resolving the summary judgment motion because 
Dworman had failed to explain why Ocwen's tax filings were material 
to his summary judgment opposition. 
On the merits, for Dworman's breach of contract claim, 
the district court concluded that the undisputed factual record 
demonstrated that the defendants did not breach the 2016 Agreement 
by failing to forgive the Deferred Principal Reduction Amount. In 
support, the court pointed to undisputed evidence that Dworman 
failed to meet the contractual conditions for loan forgiveness in 
Section 3(c) of the Agreement -- i.e., not falling more than three 
months behind on payments. The court also rejected Dworman's 

2 Dworman first raised this discovery issue at the summary 
judgment stage by filing a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56(d) 
affidavit with his opposition to the defendants' summary judgment 
motion. 
- 8 - 
argument that the defendants had waived their right to claim that 
he breached the 2016 Agreement by accepting his late mortgage 
payments. The court concluded that Section 12 of the 2016 
Agreement expressly provided that Ocwen's acceptance of late 
payments would not waive any right or remedy. 
Additionally, the district court dispensed with 
Dworman's argument that issuance of the Form 1099 -C and the 
defendants' subsequent conduct operated to discharge his debt. In 
so doing, the court cited the "majority view" that issuing a Form 
1099-C does not legally discharge a debt but rather satisfies an 
IRS reporting requirement. Likewise, the court rejected Dworman's 
claim that PHH's omission of the Deferred Principal Reduction 
Amount from the June 2019 Transfer Notice reflected forgiveness of 
that amount. The court reasoned that PHH's failure to mention the 
Deferred Principal Reduction Amount did not constitute express 
forgiveness, and it found that PHH's August 13, 2019, corrective 
letter timely accounted for the Deferred Principal Balance. 
For Dworman's claim alleging breach of the covenant of 
good faith and fair dealing, the district court determined that no 
reasonable jury could find the requisite "dishonest purpose or 
conscious wrongdoing" by the defendants. Quoting Conte v. Bank of 
Am., N.A., 52 F. Supp. 3d 265, 269 (D. Mass. 2014). To the 
contrary, the defendants attemp ted to provide Dworman with 
multiple debt relief options, engaged in good-faith conduct by 
- 9 - 
entering the 2016 Agreement, and applied the contract terms as 
written. 
Next, the district court concluded that Dworman's 
Chapter 93A claim failed for procedural and substantive reasons. 
Procedurally, Dworman's complaint failed to allege that he sent 
the required pre-suit demand letter to the defendants . 
Substantively, the court concluded that the Chapter 93A claim 
failed because it was predicated on the same insufficient breach 
arguments underlying Dworman's other claims. And even if the 
defendants had breached the 2016 Agreement , the record did not 
show the kind of egregiously wrong conduct contemplated by Chapter 
93A. 
Finally, the district court rejected Dworman's 
derivative declaratory judgment claim, reasoning that there was no 
justification to issue a declaration that the Deferred Principal 
Reduction Amount had been forgiven given the failure of his other 
claims. 
Dworman timely appealed. 
II. 
A. 
We review de novo the district court's grant 
of summary judgment. Henderson v. Mass. Bay Transp. Auth., 977 
F.3d 20, 29 (1st Cir. 2020). In conducting our review, we construe 
the facts and all reasonable inferences from those facts in favor 
- 10 - 
of the non -movant -- here, Dworman. See Pleasantdale Condos. , 
L

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Pursoo
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Pursoo 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06161 
 October 21, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Leon Pursoo, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 21, 2026 
 2025-02144, (Index No. 12192/09) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Laurence L. Love 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Hinshaw & Culbertson LLP, New York, NY (Ali Degan and Schuyler B. Kraus of counsel), for appellant. 
 Yolande I. Nicholson, P.C., Brooklyn, NY, for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Danielle M. Peterson, J.), entered January 30, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, granted that branch of the cross-motion of the defendant Leon Pursoo which was pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate an order of the same court dated July 27, 2022, granting the plaintiff's motion, among other things, for an order of reference and for leave to enter a default judgment against that defendant and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him, and denied the plaintiff's cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant Leon Pursoo. 
 ORDERED that the order entered January 30, 2025, is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In December 2009, the plaintiff's predecessor in interest, GMC Mortgage, LLC, commenced this action against, among others, the defendant Leon Pursoo (hereinafter the defendant) to foreclosure a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Westbury. The plaintiff failed to serve the defendant within 120 days of the commencement of the action. In February 2011, the plaintiff voluntarily discontinued the action. In October 2017, the plaintiff moved to vacate the voluntary discontinuance and restore the action to the active calendar, and, in an order entered April 30, 2018, the Supreme Court granted the motion. 
 On December 9, 2019, 10 years after the commencement of this action and more than 1 year after it was restored to the active calendar, the plaintiff purportedly served the defendant with the summons and complaint. In February 2020, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for an order of reference and for leave to enter a default judgment against the defendant. In an order dated July 27, 2022 (hereinafter the July 2022 order), the Supreme Court granted the motion. In January 2024, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant cross-moved, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate the July 2022 order and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. Thereafter, the plaintiff cross-moved pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. In an order entered January 30, 2025, the court, among other things, [*2] denied the plaintiff's motion, granted that branch of the defendant's cross-motion, and denied the plaintiff's cross-motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 Generally, service of a summons and complaint must be made within 120 days after the commencement of the action ( see CPLR 306-b). Whether to grant "[a]n extension of time" to effectuate "service is a matter within the court's discretion" ( Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d 95, 101). "Pursuant to CPLR 306-b, a court may, in the exercise of its discretion, grant a motion for an extension of time within which to effect service of the summons and complaint for good cause shown or in the interest of justice" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d 1070, 1072; see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Martinez , 211 AD3d 909, 911). "Good cause and interest of justice are two separate and independent statutory standards" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d 1012, 1013). Good cause requires a showing of reasonable diligence in attempting to effect service ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d at 1072; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d at 1014). In deciding whether to grant a motion to extend the time for service in the interest of justice, the court must carefully analyze "the factual setting of the case and . . . balanc[e] . . . the competing interests presented by the parties. Unlike an extension request premised on good cause, a plaintiff need not establish reasonably diligent efforts at service as a threshold matter" ( Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105). "Under the interest of justice standard, 'the court may consider diligence, or lack thereof, along with any other relevant factor in making its determination, including expiration of the Statute of Limitations, the meritorious nature of the cause of action, the length of delay in service, the promptness of a plaintiff's request for the extension of time, and prejudice to defendant'" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gewirtz , 204 AD3d at 1072, quoting Leader v Maroney, Ponzini & Spencer , 97 NY2d at 105-106). 
 Here, the plaintiff did not contend that it attempted to serve the defendant within 120 days of the commencement of this action and, therefore, failed to show good cause for an extension of time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Fameux , 201 AD3d at 1014). Additionally, the plaintiff failed to establish that an extension of time was warranted in the interest of justice. The plaintiff failed to offer any excuse for its delay of approximately 15 years from the commencement of this action to move to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. Moreover, the plaintiff submitted no evidence that the defendant had actual notice of the action within 120 days of its commencement ( see id. ; Federal Natl. Mtge. Assn. v Cassis , 187 AD3d 1145, 1147). Accordingly, the court properly denied the plaintiff's cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. 
 Since the defendant was not properly served with the summons and complaint and the plaintiff failed to demonstrate entitlement to an extension of time to effectuate service, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was pursuant to CPLR 5015 to vacate the July 2022 order and, upon vacatur, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Labin , 232 AD3d 861, 865; see Citimortgage, Inc. v Unger , 230 AD3d 1226, 1227) and denied the plaintiff's motion for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. 
 DILLON, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, LOVE and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank N.A. v. Vetri
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank N.A. v Vetri 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06162 
 October 21, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 William L. Vetri, etc., appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 21, 2026 
 2025-01357, 2025-01358, (Index No. 67745/14) 
 Angela G. Iannacci, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Carl J. Landicino 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 James F. Misiano, P.C., Brentwood, NY, for appellant. 
 Roach & Lin, P.C., Syosset, NY (Hans H. Augustin of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant William L. Vetri appeals from two orders of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (S. Betsy Heckman Torres, J.), both dated December 10, 2024. The first order, insofar as appealed from, denied that defendant's cross-motion pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(2) and (3) to vacate an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the same court (Denise F. Molia, J.) dated December 4, 2017, and thereupon, to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the second order is dismissed as abandoned; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the first order is affirmed insofar as appealed from; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the plaintiff. 
 In September 2014, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant William L. Vetri (hereinafter the defendant) to foreclose a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Suffolk County. The defendant interposed an answer in which he asserted various affirmative defenses, including lack of standing. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant and for an order of reference. The defendant did not oppose that motion. In an order dated December 20, 2016, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion. The plaintiff then moved, among other things, for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant did not oppose that motion. In an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale dated December 4, 2017, the court, inter alia, granted that motion and directed the sale of the property. 
 In October 2024, the plaintiff moved, among other things, to extend the time to conduct the foreclosure sale. The defendant cross-moved pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(2) and (3) to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale and, thereupon, to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him for lack of standing. In an order dated December 10, 2024, the [*2] Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the defendant's cross-motion. The defendant appeals. We affirm the order insofar as appealed from, albeit on grounds different from those relied upon by the Supreme Court. 
 The Supreme Court properly denied that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(2) to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. "The court which rendered a judgment or order may relieve a party from it . . . upon the ground of . . . newly-discovered evidence which, if introduced at the trial, would probably have produced a different result" ( id. ). Here, the defendant failed to demonstrate that the purported newly discovered evidence would probably have produced a different result ( see JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Borukhov , 203 AD3d 808, 809). 
 The Supreme Court also properly denied that branch of the defendant's cross-motion which was pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) to vacate the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale. CPLR 5015(a)(3) permits a court to relieve a party from an order or judgment on the ground of "fraud, misrepresentation, or other misconduct of an adverse party." Here, the defendant's contentions amount to allegations of intrinsic fraud ( see Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Marte , 219 AD3d 929, 930; U.S. Bank N.A. v Carucci , 217 AD3d 894, 895). "A defendant seeking to vacate a default pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) based on intrinsic fraud must establish both a reasonable excuse for the default and a potentially meritorious defense to the action" ( Caridi v Tanico , 188 AD3d 636, 637 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Karlis , 138 AD3d 915, 916). The defendant failed to provide a potentially meritorious defense to the action ( see Bank of Am. N.A. v Patino , 128 AD3d 994, 994). Moreover, the defendant also failed to establish that the plaintiff engaged in any fraud, misrepresentation, or other misconduct in securing the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see U.S. Bank, N.A. v Guaman , 238 AD3d 941, 942; Bank of Am. N.A. v Patino , 128 AD3d at 994). 
 Since the defendant raises no argument in his brief regarding his appeal from a second order dated December 10, 2024, we must dismiss the appeal from that order as abandoned ( see Mazzurco v Gordon , 173 AD3d 1001, 1003). 
 The parties' remaining contentions either are without merit or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 IANNACCI, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, LANDICINO and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: U.S. Bank, N.A. v. Nektalov
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
U.S. Bank, N.A. v Nektalov 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06163 
 October 21, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 U.S. Bank, National Association, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Boris Nektalov, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 21, 2026 
 2025-01027, (Index No. 701242/13) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Linda Christopher 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LLP, New York, NY (Brian P. Scibetta and Kyra Mercadier of counsel), for appellant. 
 Law Office of Henry Graham, P.C., Greenvale, NY (Henry M. Graham of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Scott Dunn, J.), entered August 13, 2024. The order granted the motion of the defendant Boris Nektalov pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as abandoned. 
 ORDERED that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the motion of the defendant Boris Nektalov pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as abandoned is denied. 
 In April 2013, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendant Boris Nektalov (hereinafter the defendant), among others, to foreclose a mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Queens. In July 2013, after the defendant failed to interpose an answer or otherwise timely appear in the action, the plaintiff filed a request for judicial intervention, seeking a foreclosure settlement conference, among other things. On September 3, 2013, the matter was released from the foreclosure settlement conference part. 
 In June 2014, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against a different defendant and, as against all defendants, for an order of reference. The Supreme Court denied that motion in an order dated September 16, 2014. 
 In April 2022, the defendant moved pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as abandoned. The plaintiff opposed the defendant's motion. In an order entered August 13, 2024, the Supreme Court granted the defendant's motion. The plaintiff appeals. 
 CPLR 3215(c) provides that if a plaintiff fails to take proceedings for the entry of judgment within one year after the default of a defendant, the court shall not enter judgment but shall dismiss the complaint as abandoned, unless sufficient cause is shown why the complaint should not be dismissed ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Wint , 235 AD3d 701, 702-703; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Campbell , 219 AD3d 701, 703). To avoid dismissal pursuant to CPLR 3215(c), it is not necessary for a plaintiff to actually obtain a judgment within one year after the default, nor is a plaintiff required to specifically seek the entry of a judgment within a year ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Wint , 235 AD3d at 703; Citibank, N.A. v Kerszko , 203 AD3d 42, 51). "Rather, as long as [*2] proceedings are being taken, and these proceedings manifest an intent not to abandon the case but to seek a judgment, the case should not be subject to dismissal" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Attard , 197 AD3d 619, 620-621 [alteration and internal quotation marks omitted]; see Cumanet, LLC v Murad , 188 AD3d 1149, 1151). Further, where an action is subject to a mandatory settlement conference ( see CPLR 3408), the one-year deadline imposed by CPLR 3215(c) is tolled while settlement conferences are pending ( see Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Attard , 197 AD3d at 621; Cumanet, LLC v Murad , 188 AD3d at 1151). 
 Here, the plaintiff initiated proceedings for the entry of a judgment against the defendant by moving, inter alia, for an order of reference in June 2014, which was well within one year after the matter was released from the foreclosure settlement conference part ( see Citibank, N.A. v Kerszko , 203 AD3d at 51-52; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Attard , 197 AD3d at 621; cf. LaSalle Bank N.A. v Benjamin , 164 AD3d 1223, 1224). That the motion was denied was irrelevant for purposes of satisfying CPLR 3215(c) ( see Bank of N.Y. v Ilonzeh , 203 AD3d 1119, 1121; Citibank, N.A. v Kerszko , 203 AD3d at 52). "It is enough that the plaintiff timely takes the preliminary step toward obtaining a default judgment of foreclosure and sale by moving for an order of reference to establish that it initiated proceedings for entry of a judgment within one year of the default for the purposes of satisfying CPLR 3215(c)" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Khalil , 208 AD3d 555, 557-558 [alteration and internal quotation marks omitted]; see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Wint , 235 AD3d at 703). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion pursuant to CPLR 3215(c) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him as abandoned. 
 The parties' remaining contentions need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., CHRISTOPHER, WARHIT and GOLIA, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: VK Dental Group, Inc. v. Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
VK Dental Group, Inc. v Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06164 
 October 21, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 VK Dental Group, Inc., respondent, 
 v 
 Tender Touch Physical Therapy, PLLC, et al., appellants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 21, 2026 
 2024-12535, 2025-00245, (Index No. 513787/22) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Laurence L. Love 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Kahn Yuniver Law, Brooklyn, NY (Steven R. Yuniver and Bhargava Kosuru of counsel), for appellants. 
 Treybich Law, P.C., New York, NY (Michael Treybich of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to recover damages for breach of contract, the defendants appeal from (1) an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Robin K. Sheares, J.), dated October 21, 2024, and (2) a judgment of the same court dated November 21, 2024. The order, after a hearing, granted the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the complaint. The judgment, upon the order, is in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendants in the total sum of $1,004,426.20. 
 ORDERED that the appeal from the order is dismissed; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that the judgment is reversed, on the law, the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the complaint is denied, and the order dated October 21, 2024, is modified accordingly; and it is further, 
 ORDERED that one bill of costs is awarded to the defendants. 
 In January 2017, nonparty Metrotech Smile Dental, P.C. (hereinafter Metrotech), entered into an agreement to lease certain real property from nonparty 350 Fulton Realty, LLC. In March 2017, Metrotech entered into agreements to sublease the rented premises to the defendants. In April 2018, Metrotech assigned its lease to the plaintiff, which assumed the role of sublessor to the defendants. 
 In May 2022, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendants to recover damages for breach of the sublease agreements, alleging that the defendants failed to pay rent owed, resulting in the plaintiff being forced to surrender possession of the leased premises. Thereafter, the plaintiff moved for summary judgment on the complaint. In an order dated October 21, 2024, after a hearing, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion. The court subsequently issued a judgment in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendants in the total sum of $1,004,426.20. The defendants appeal. 
 The appeal from the order must be dismissed because the right of direct appeal therefrom terminated with the entry of the judgment in the action ( see Matter of Aho , 39 NY2d 241, [*2] 248). The issues raised on the appeal from the order are brought up for review and have been considered on the appeal from the judgment ( see CPLR 5501[a][1]). 
 To recover damages for breach of contract, a plaintiff must demonstrate the existence of a contract, the plaintiff's performance pursuant to the contract, the defendant's breach of its contractual obligations, and damages resulting from the breach ( Beacon Sales Acquisition, Inc. v Hudson Val. Renovations, LLC , 247 AD3d 1113, 1114; see Shulamith Sch. for Girls, Inc. v Schulamith Sch. for Girls of Brooklyn , 230 AD3d 822, 823-824). 
 Here, even assuming, arguendo, that the Supreme Court improperly conducted a hearing to aid in the determination of the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment, at which live testimony was heard from a witness for the plaintiff, the plaintiff established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law without consideration of the testimony elicited at the hearing. The plaintiff satisfied its prima facie burden by submitting evidence showing that the defendants breached their obligation under the sublease agreements to pay the plaintiff rent for certain months ( see ENY Rockaway, LLC v W 16 E. N.Y., LLC , 244 AD3d 689, 692). In opposition, however, the defendants raised a triable issue of fact as to whether the plaintiff failed to perform its obligations under the terms of the sublease agreements by submitting the affidavit of their principal, Svetlana Kibrik, who averred that the plaintiff failed to comply with its obligations under the sublease agreements to pay for 50% of utilities and by having gas service disconnected to the subleased premises ( see LD Exch., Inc. v Orion Telecom. Corp. , 302 AD2d 565). 
 In light of our determination, we need not reach the parties' remaining contentions. 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the complaint. 
 DILLON, J.P., WOOTEN, LOVE and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur.

leads.caseName: Geographic Computer Technologies, L.L.C. Versus Thomas Nourse
leads.text:
26-C-468 
Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal 
State of Louisiana 

No. 26-C-468 

GEOGRAPHIC COMPUTER TECHNOLOGIES, L.L.C. 

versus 

THOMAS NOURSE 

IN RE GEOGRAPHIC COMPUTER TECHNOLOGIES, L.L.C. 
APPLYING FOR SUPERVISORY WRIT FROM THE TWENTY -FOURTH JUDICIAL DISTRICT 
COURT, PARISH OF JEFFERSON, STATE OF LOUISIANA, DIRECTED TO THE HONORABLE 
FRANK A. BRINDISI, DIVISION "E", NUMBER 879-025 

Panel composed of Judges Susan M. Chehardy, 
Marc E. Johnson, and John J. Molaison, Jr. 

WRIT GRANTED; JUDGMENT REVERSED; EXCEPTION 
OVERRULED; ORDER OF TRANSFER VACATED; REMANDED 

Relator, Geographic Computer Technologies, L.L.C. (“GCT”), seeks 
supervisory review of the district court’s judgment of September 21, 2026, which 
sustained the declinatory exception of improper venue filed by respondent, Thomas 
Nourse, and ordered this action transferred to Caddo Parish. For the reasons that 
follow, we grant the writ, reverse the judgment, overrule the exception, vacate the 
order of transfer, and remand for further proceedings. 
Facts and Procedural History 
 GCT is a Louisiana limited liability company domiciled in Jefferson Parish, 
with its sole office and principal place of business in Metairie; all of its employees 

October 21, 2026 

2 

work in Jefferson Parish. The respondent, Mr. Nourse, is an individual domiciled 
in Caddo Parish. Mr. Nourse was GCT’s salaried software developer and 
infrastructure administrator until November 1, 2025, and worked principally from 
his home in Caddo Parish. 
On August 13, 2026, GCT sued Mr. Nourse in the Twenty-Fourth Judicial 
District Court, asserting claims for breach of the duty of loyalty, violation of the 
Louisiana Unfair Trade Practices Act, La. R.S. 51:1401 et seq., conversion, unjust 
enrichment in the alternative, and injunctive relief. GCT pleaded that venue lies in 
Jefferson Parish under La. C.C.P. art. 74 because it sustained damages there and 
because the wrongful conduct caused injury there. 
Mr. Nourse filed a declinatory exception of improper venue. At the 
September 2, 2026 hearing, GCT presented two witnesses and introduced 
documentary exhibits, which the court admitted without objection; Mr. Nourse 
offered no evidence. GCT’s uncontroverted showing established that Mr. Nourse 
installed and configured GCT’s GIS Data Updater on the workstation of a GCT 
employee located in River Ridge, within Jefferson Parish, and directed that update 
tasks be run from that workstation. It further established that GCT, domiciled in 
Jefferson Parish and maintaining no other office, sustained its economic losses 
there, including payments of $72,940 made from Jefferson Parish and its 
investigation and remediation costs. The district court sustained the exception and 
ordered the matter transferred to Caddo Parish, referring to La. C.C.P. arts. 42 and 
74 and to the physical locations of the defendant and the computer hardware. 
 GCT timely filed the instant writ application. 
Standard of Review 
An exception of improper venue presents a question of law, which this Court 
reviews de novo and resolves on the record without deference to the district court’s 
legal conclusions. Bruno v. CDC Auto Transp., Inc., 19-1065 (La. App. 4 Cir. 

3 

6/3/20), 302 So.3d 8, 12, writ denied, 20-836 (La. 10/14/20), 302 So.3d 1118. 
When a party introduces evidence at the hearing on a declinatory exception, the 
court resolves the exception on that evidence rather than on the allegations of the 
petition. Johnson v. Byrd, 48,411 (La. App. 2 Cir. 9/25/13), 125 So.3d 1220, 1226. 
A manifest-error standard then attaches to the district court’s underlying factual 
findings. Murray v. Universal Parking & Transp., LLC, 24-787 (La. App. 4 Cir. 
7/8/25), 420 So.3d 132, 149. However, as discussed below, that deferential 
overlay has no application here. GCT’s evidence stood uncontroverted, Mr. 
Nourse offered none, and the district court made no factual findings to which 
deference could attach. The venue question therefore turns entirely on the legal 
effect of undisputed facts, which we review de novo. Bruno, 302 So.3d at 12. 
Law and Analysis 
The general rule of venue is that an action against an individual domiciled in 
this state shall be brought in the parish of his domicile. La. C.C.P. art. 42. That 
general rule is subject to the exceptions provided in Articles 71 through 85, and 
where Articles 42 and 71 through 77 conflict, the plaintiff may bring the action in 
any venue provided by any applicable article. Jumonville v. White, 07-2589 (La. 
App. 1 Cir. 5/8/08), 992 So.2d 1044, 1046 (per curiam). Mr. Nourse’s domicile in 
Caddo Parish therefore establishes that parish as a venue of right, but it does not 
foreclose GCT’s reliance on an applicable exception. 
GCT’s claims for breach of the duty of loyalty, unfair trade practices, 
conversion, and unjust enrichment are delictual in nature and seek the recovery of 
damages for an offense or quasi-offense. The governing exception is La. C.C.P. 
art. 74, which provides that such an action “may be brought in the parish where the 
wrongful conduct occurred, or in the parish where the damages were sustained” 
and that an action to enjoin an offense or quasi-offense may be brought in the 
parish where the wrongful conduct occurred or may occur. Article 74 is 

4 

disjunctive: venue is proper if either the place of the wrongful conduct or the place 
where the damages were sustained lies in the forum parish. This Court has applied 
Article 74 to the precise setting this case presents — a former employer's delictual 
claims against a former employee for breach of fiduciary duty and unfair trade 
practices — and has fixed venue in the parish where the employee committed the 
wrongful conduct during his employment. See Novelaire Techs., L.L.C. v. 
Harrison, 06-94 (La. App. 5 Cir. 7/25/06), 939 So.2d 437, 443. 
Applying that text to the uncontroverted record, we conclude that Jefferson 
Parish is a parish of proper venue under article 74’s damages prong. 
First, GCT sustained its damages in Jefferson Parish. The loss is not an 
abstraction felt wherever GCT happens to reside; it consists of concrete, locatable 
events. GCT disbursed the $72,940 in payments at issue from Jefferson Parish and 
performed and paid for its investigation and remediation work there. Those acts 
fixed the situs of the economic injury, and they occurred in Jefferson Parish 
independently of where GCT is domiciled. This is the direct, readily established 
loss that Article 74’s “damages sustained” prong contemplates, not the kind of 
nebulous or derivative injury — felt by a plaintiff wherever it happens to be — that 
cannot anchor venue. See Coursey v. White, 184 So.2d 625, 627 (La. App. 4 Cir. 
1966). That GCT maintains no other office confirms that Jefferson Parish is where 
the loss landed. Under the plain language of Article 74, that parish is a parish of 
proper venue. 
Second, a portion of the alleged wrongful conduct occurred in Jefferson 
Parish. The uncontroverted evidence shows that Mr. Nourse installed and 
configured the instrumentality of the alleged diversion — GCT’s GIS Data 
Updater — on a GCT workstation physically located in River Ridge, Jefferson 
Parish, and directed that the tasks be run from that workstation. That Mr. Nourse 

5 

performed some of these acts by remote connection from Caddo Parish does not 
displace the site of the instrumentality and its operation in Jefferson Parish. 
Based on the foregoing, we find that the district court erred as a matter of 
law. After correctly identifying Article 74 as the applicable exception, the court 
resolved venue by reference to the physical location of the defendant and of the 
computer hardware, rather than by application of the statute’s “damages sustained” 
and “wrongful conduct” prongs to the uncontroverted record. On de novo review, 
and because GCT’s evidence stood uncontroverted, we find that Jefferson Parish is 
a parish of proper venue under Article 74. 
Because Article 74 independently establishes proper venue in Jefferson 
Parish, we need not reach GCT’s alternative contention under La. C.C.P. art. 76.1, 
nor its assignments of error concerning ancillary venue and leave to amend under 
La. C.C.P. art. 932(A). Likewise, because we hold that venue is proper, no 
occasion arises to consider transfer or dismissal under La. C.C.P. arts. 121 and 
932; those articles govern only when a plaintiff brings an action in a court of 
improper venue. 
Decree 
For these reasons, we grant the writ application, reverse the September 21, 
2026 judgment sustaining the declinatory exception of improper venue, overrule 
the exception, and vacate the order transferring this action to Caddo Parish. We 
remand the matter for further proceedings consistent with this disposition. 
Gretna, Louisiana, this 21st day of October, 2026.

leads.text:
J-A21016-26 

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION - SEE SUPERIOR COURT O.P. 65.37 

TP INVESTMENT PROPERTIES, LLC 

 v. 

NAAMA, LLC, HAWAH MUSA, AND ACT 
LAND SERVICES, LLC 

APPEAL OF: NAAMA, LLC 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
 PENNSYLVANIA 

No. 3084 EDA 2025 

Appeal from the Judgment Entered November 24, 2025 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County Civil Division at 
No(s): 230300561 

BEFORE: LAZARUS, P.J., BECK, J., and NEUMAN, J. 
MEMORANDUM BY LAZARUS, P.J.: FILED OCTOBER 21, 2026 
 Defendant Naama, LLC (Naama), appeals from the judgment, entered 
in favor of Plaintiff TP Investment Properties, LLC (TP), in the Court of 
Common Pleas of Philadelphia County, following a non-jury trial. Because TP 
was an innocent bona fide purchaser without notice, see 21 P.S. § 351, and 
Naama waited 10 months to record its interests in the subject property, id. at 
§§ 444, 621, we affirm. 
 TP is a Philadelphia real estate investment company; Tyler Phillips is 
TP’s principal. Naama is a Wyoming limited liability company that operates as 
a residential property holding company; Naama’s managing partner/owner is 
Kotb “Sam” Elbialy. Naama is also the parent company of Homemart, LLC. 
Third-party defendant, ACT Land Services, LLC (ACT), is a Philadelphia title 
search company. 
J-A21016-26 
- 2 - 
On March 6, 2023, TP filed a quiet title action against Naama and 
Defendant Hawah Musa (Musa) in connection with the sale of a residential 
property (the Property) located at 2823 N. 28th Street, Philadelphia.1 See 
Pa.R.C.P. 1061(b). TP’s complaint alleged that on January 2, 2023, Musa 
executed a general warrant deed (Deed) conveying the Property to TP for 
$75,000.00. The Deed names Musa as the grantee of the Property. See 
Complaint, 3/6/23, at 1. At the closing of the sale of the Property on January 
13, 2023, the Deed was transferred to TP. On January 23, 2023, the Deed 
was recorded in the Philadelphia Department of Records. 
The complaint alleged that, following the closing on the Property on 
January 23, 2023, “a mortgage [(Naama Mortgage), dated March 21, 2022, 
on the Property] was purportedly granted by Defendant Musa in favor of 
Defendant Naama [and] was recorded[.]” Id., at 3. The complaint also 
alleged that a deed in lieu of foreclosure (Naama Deed) on the Property, dated
