leads.caseName: Ruth A. Fuessley, Neal Gilbertson, and Stephanie Gilbertson v. City of Cedar Rapids
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF IOWA
 _______________

 No. 25-1295
 Filed October 21, 2026
 _______________

 Ruth A. Fuessley, Neal Gilbertson, and Stephanie Gilbertson
 Plaintiffs–Appellants,
 v.
 City of Cedar Rapids, Iowa,
 Defendant–Appellee.
 _______________

 Appeal from the Iowa District Court for Linn County,
 The Honorable Michael Harris, Judge.
 _______________

 AFFIRMED
 _______________

Daniel L. Manning Sr. (argued) of Peddicord Lillis LLP, West Des Moines,
 attorney for appellants.

Patrick T. Burk (argued) and Allison M. Steuterman of Brick Gentry, P.C.,
 West Des Moines,
 attorneys for appellee.
 _______________

 Heard at oral argument
 by Tabor, C.J., and Schumacher and Buller, JJ.
 Opinion by Buller, J.

 1
 BULLER, Judge.

 Neighbors Ruth Fuessley and Neal and Stephanie Gilbertson appeal
the condemnation of their properties as part of the Cedar River flood control
project in Cedar Rapids. Because acquisition of the properties is reasonably
necessary to obtain necessary permits and accreditation, and the properties
are necessary to achieve the flood control system, we affirm.

 BACKGROUND FACTS
 In June 2008, the City of Cedar Rapids (the City) experienced a 1,000-
year flood, devastating the City as the Cedar River overflowed its banks,
cresting at more than thirty-one feet—nineteen feet above flood level. The
flooding river spread to a mile wide through downtown Cedar Rapids,
damaging hundreds of businesses and public buildings costing more than
$5.4 billion.

 As recovery efforts were underway, the City began planning a flood
control project to prevent similar flooding in the future. The City worked
with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (the Corps) to create a Flood Control
System (FCS) Master Plan, which guides the development of seven and a
half miles of flood control along the Cedar River—3.8 miles on the east side
to be built by the Corps, and 3.7 miles of levees and flood walls on the west
bank of the river under the City’s purview. The FCS “creates an
impenetrable area where the water is forced to stay in the river”—
constraining its width to two-tenths of a mile through the downtown area.

 At the northern, upstream edge of the FCS area—which was hit hard
by the 2008 flood—Fuessley and the Gilbertsons own neighboring properties
backing up to the river. Since the original 2016 Master Plan, both properties
had been designated as “Full Acquisition Property” with the levee originally

 2
 extending onto the Gilbertsons’ property and construction expected on
Fuessley’s property. In 2017, the City sent an acquisition option letter to the
Gilbertsons; Fuessley was first contacted in 2018. Fuessley and the City
(through a contractor) negotiated the City’s offer, but they were unable to
reach an agreement; the Gilbertsons generally did not respond to the City’s
attempts and refused the appraisal amount in early 2023.

 In 2021, as the early sections of the project reached completion, the
City moved to begin implementation of the FCS in all remaining segments,
including acquisition of the properties needed for the remaining
construction. In December 2022, the north edge of the FCS was revised,
moving the levee edge south and adding a floodwall that turned inland to
connect with the east-west levee just south of the properties. The revised
FCS plan would reroute their street starting north of their properties,
sending the road up a new embankment in front of their homes, over a
sixteen-foot-high levee just south and west of the properties, then down
another embankment to rejoin the existing road on the other side. This plan
leaves the properties in a small triangle of land bound by the embankment to
the west, levee and floodwall to the south, and the river to the northeast. The
revised FCS continued to designate Fuessley’s and the Gilbertsons’
properties as “Full Acquisition.”

 The property owners contested the City’s right to condemn their
properties, arguing it was not necessary under the revised FCS plan. At a
hearing on the matter, the City had the burden “to prove by a preponderance
of the evidence” their reason for condemnation met the definition of “public
use, public purpose, or public improvement.” Iowa Code § 6A.24(3) (2023).
The City presented testimony from the FCS manager and their expert
witness, a flood risk and water infrastructure engineering consultant who had

 3
 facilitated the design and permitting of the FCS. The property owners
offered their own experts, including an engineer specializing in floodplain
analysis.

 A new flow frequency study estimated the Fuessley and Gilbertson
properties’ 100-year base flood elevations (BFE) were 3.4 feet higher than
current expected flood levels. The FCS would separately cause an additional
0.3 foot increase in the properties’ BFE; that increase is a problem under
state and federal regulations establishing parameters for construction
affecting existing structures in a floodplain for safety and insurability. While
the property owners’ expert emphasized the regulations do not require
removal of the structures, he did not contest their presence could preclude
the Iowa Department of Natural Resources (DNR) permitting the project or
the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) issuing a new Letter
of Map Revision (LOMR).

 The district court found that the properties “are not located within the
project area”—i.e., their removal is not necessary for the physical
construction of the FCS. But the court observed that fact “does not, by itself,
prove that the taking of the properties would not be necessary for the
completion of the FCS” and the taking could still be done for a public
purpose. The court pinpointed testimony indicating the DNR would not
issue the necessary permit to construct that portion of the FCS while
structures remain on the properties, and that the community at large benefits
from the impact on flood-insurance requirements. The court found the City
proved by a preponderance of evidence the taking of the properties was for a
public purpose. Fuessley and the Gilbertsons appeal.

 4
  STANDARD OF REVIEW
 Fuessley and the Gilbertsons argue our review is of the district court’s
statutory construction, so for correction of errors at law. Brendeland v. Iowa
Dep’t of Transp., 14 N.W.3d 135, 142 (Iowa 2024). The City counters that the
action was tried in equity, so our review would be de novo. Iowa R. App.
P. 6.907. To the extent our review hinges on statutory interpretation, we
review for errors at law. We review that which is not a legal question de novo.

 DISCUSSION
 Fuessley and the Gilbertsons assert the district court erred in denying
their challenges to the condemnation. As we understand their argument on
appeal, since the 2022 FCS plan revision altered the north end of the western
FCS, they believe their properties are no longer in the physical footprint of
the FCS, necessary to its construction, or mandatory acquisitions subject to
the City’s condemnation powers, so the City could not legally condemn their
property. They instead urge the City and FCS should accommodate their
existing structures. The City counters that condemning the properties is
necessary to obtain permits for that segment of the FCS and to effectuate a
reduction in flood insurance rates benefitting the City’s general public under
the FEMA Insurance Program. For the reasons that follow, we affirm the
district court’s conclusion that the condemnation was proper.

 I. Case Law

 Cities have the “right to take private property for public use . . . for
public purposes which are reasonable and necessary as an incident to the
powers and duties conferred upon cities.” Iowa Code § 6A.4(6); see ACCO
Unlimited Corp. v. City of Johnston, 611 N.W.2d 506, 510 (Iowa 2000). The
burden is on the City “to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the

 5
 finding of public use, public purpose, or public improvement meets the
definition of those terms.” Iowa Code § 6A.24(3). “An absolute necessity for
taking the particular land need not exist. A reasonable necessity is sufficient.”
Vittetoe v. Iowa S. Utils. Co., 123 N.W.2d 878, 881 (Iowa 1963).

 “[W]ater and its control are obviously of paramount importance to the
welfare of the people.” Iowa Nat. Res. Council v. Van Zee, 158 N.W.2d 111, 118
(Iowa 1968). “Proper control of rivers and streams, of course, involves the
exercise of control of the use of property adjoining these streams or in the
recognized floodway or flood plains. Police power properly regulates use of
that property because uncontrolled use would be harmful to the public
interest.” Id.

 When applying to condemn a property, a city must show
 the minimum amount of land necessary to achieve the public purpose and
 the amount of land to be acquired by condemnation for the public
 improvement. Any land to be acquired by condemnation beyond the
 necessary minimum to complete the project shall be presumed not to be
 necessary for a public use or public purpose unless the applicant can show
 that a substantial need exists for the additional property to achieve the
 public use or public purpose. . . .

Iowa Code § 6B.3(1)(g).

 There is no question the FCS as a whole falls within the chapter-6B
definition of “public use, public purpose, or public improvement.”

 II. The City’s Need

 We next consider the City’s need, focusing on two obstacles faced by
the City if it did not condemn the properties: permitting and accreditation.

 6
  A. Permitting

 Fuessley and the Gilbertsons argue the City exceeded its authority to
condemn the properties and failed to prove the properties were part of “the
minimum amount necessary to accomplish the stated public purpose”—in
this case the construction of the FCS. At trial, the City argued it needed to
condemn the properties in order to obtain the permits from the State
necessary to build that portion of the FCS. The Fuessley and Gilbertson
properties were already located within the portion of the floodplain at risk of
significant flooding, and the FCS design placed them within the floodway (an
area reserved for conveyance of flood flows). See Iowa Admin. Code
r. 567-75.4 (2023).1

 The City is required by law to obtain appropriate permits from the
DNR to construct the FCS. Iowa Code § 455B.277(1); Iowa Admin. Code
r. 567–71.4(2). As part of establishing a floodway, to the extent feasible, the
encroachment is “to avoid the need to seek removal of a lawful existing
structure,” to minimize any increase in BFE where it would affect an existing
structure, and to avoid structures in the floodway if it would limit
improvements or replacement of the structure. Id. r. 567-75.4(3). Both the
FCS manager and the City’s consultant testified that the structures’
presence was affecting the City’s ability to obtain the needed DNR permits.

 So while the property owners are correct that the DNR has not
“mandated” the City condemn the properties, the refusal to issue permits
while the structures stand is also binding and a determining factor in the

 1
 This chapter of administrative regulations was rescinded in 2025 and rewritten
into chapter 70. But we consider the regulations in effect at the time this action was
brought and use the then-existing numbering.

 7
 City’s actions. Given the magnitude of the project, the backwater effect2 on
the properties, the presence of the road embankment, and the impossibility
of extending the flood protections beyond the properties without destroying
the structures during the construction process,3 it is not feasible to leave the
current structures intact. See Iowa Admin. Code r. 567-72.1, -72.11, -75.4. So
properties necessary to obtain the permit would fall within “the minimum
amount of land necessary” or those substantially needed to achieve the
public purpose of the FCS. See Iowa Code § 6B.3(1)(g).

 B. FEMA Accreditation

 To qualify for a LOMR from FEMA, the community must “[c]ertif[y]
that no structures are located in areas which would be impacted by the
in

leads.caseName: Bianca Rampartap v. Darryl Rampartap
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA
 FOURTH DISTRICT

 BIANCA RAMPARTAP,
 Appellant,

 v.

 DARRYL RAMPARTAP,
 Appellee.

 No. 4D2025-1920

 [October 21, 2026]

 Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit,
Broward County; Lauren M. Alperstein, Judge; L.T. Case No.
062016DR000326AXXXCE.

 Samuel Alexander of Alexander Appellate Law P.A., Jacksonville, for
appellant.

 No appearance for appellee.

SHEPHERD, J.

 The former wife appeals from the trial court’s final judgment, arguing
the trial court erred in three respects by: (1) imputing income to her
without notice and an opportunity to be heard; (2) adopting the
recommended order without allowing her a hearing and an opportunity to
object; and (3) imputing income to her based on contributions from her
new spouse. We reverse the improper inclusion of the new spouse’s
mortgage and household expenses contributions as those were not
payments to the former wife and therefore not within the definition of
“income” in the relevant statute. We affirm on the other two issues.

 Background

 In 2016, the parties divorced by a final judgment of dissolution. The
final judgment ordered equal timesharing for the one minor child,
established a parenting plan, and ordered that the costs of extra-curricular
activities, uniforms and equipment for those activities and summer camp
be paid 40% by the former wife and 60% by the former husband. The trial
court did not order child support at that time.
  In 2018, the trial court ordered the former husband to pay $225.42
bimonthly in child support. The trial court also modified the costs of extra-
curricular activities, uniforms and equipment for those activities and
summer camp to be paid 50% by the former wife and 50% by the former
husband.

 In 2024, the former wife filed a supplemental petition for modification
of child support and full custody. The former wife alleged that the former
husband had moved out of the country and had ceased exercising
overnight timesharing upon which child support was predicated. The trial
court granted the petition, finding that the former husband had not
exercised any timesharing in eight months, and unrebutted testimony had
established that the former husband was permanently living in Trinidad.
The trial court awarded the former wife sole parental responsibility and
100% timesharing and decision-making authority. The trial court referred
the child support issue to a hearing officer.

 The hearing officer subsequently issued a recommended order on child
support that provided, in part:

 [The former wife] testified that she earns $1,500 per month in
 gross income. In addition, [the former wife’s current] husband
 pays all of the household expenses listed in section A of her
 Financial Affidavit filed August 15, 2024, totaling $8,600 per
 month. This amount is considered income for purposes of
 calculating child support. See Varchetti v. Varchetti[,] 355 So.
 3d 435 (Fla. 4[th] DCA 2023). The undersigned finds that [the
 former wife] has a gross (sic) monthly income of $10,100 and
 a net (sic) monthly income of $10,487.

 ....

 [The former husband’s] currently (sic) child support obligation
 totals $270.42 which includes $225.42 for current child
 support and $45 towards the child support arrears. [The
 former wife] is entitled to retroactive child support to August
 15, 2024 when the Petition for Modification was filed.
 Therefore, [the former husband] owes $1,953.38 ($403 -
 $225.42 = $177.58 x 11 months) in retroactive child support.

 The trial court adopted the hearing officer’s findings and ordered child
support as follows:

 2
  [T]he former husband to pay ongoing child support for the
 parties’ minor child in the amount of $403 per month,
 commencing July 1, 2025 and a like sum shall be paid on the
 1st day of each month until February 28, 2030 or until such
 time as the oldest/child dies, joins the armed forces, or
 otherwise becomes emancipated, whichever first occurs.... The
 child support obligation may continue beyond the age of 18 and
 until high school graduation for any child who is: dependent in
 fact; between the ages of 18 and 19; and is still in high school,
 performing in good faith with a reasonable expectation of
 graduation before the age of 19. The [former husband] owes
 retroactive child support [of] $1,953.38 through June 2025.
 These sums shall be paid in addition to the ongoing obligation
 at the rate of $81 per month until paid in full.

 The hearing officer calculated child support as demonstrated in the
child support guidelines worksheet. The hearing officer found the former
wife’s gross monthly income was $10,100 and her net monthly income was
$10,487. We believe the hearing officer incorrectly transposed those
numbers, as net income will always be less than gross income by
definition. The hearing officer then added the former wife’s incorrectly
stated $10,487 net monthly income to the former husband’s $2,551 net
monthly income, for a total net monthly income of $13,038. The hearing
officer then calculated the percentages of each parent’s income relative to
the total income, applied those percentages (80.43% for the former wife
and 19.57% for the former husband) to the monthly obligation for the one
minor child and determined that the former wife’s share of the monthly
obligation was $1,278 and the former husband’s share was $311. After
the hearing officer calculated the additional support costs and statutory
adjustments or credits, the former husband was obligated to pay $403 in
monthly child support.

 The trial court later entered a final judgment adopting the hearing
officer’s recommended order.

 One day after entry of the final judgment, the former wife filed a motion
to vacate, arguing that the trial court had failed to comply with Florida
Family Law Rule of Procedure 12.491(f) by adopting the hearing officer’s
recommended order before affording the former wife time to object. The
former wife also argued that the trial court had improperly imputed income
to her based on contributions from her new spouse. The trial court denied
the motion as legally insufficient.

 The former wife filed a motion for rehearing or amendment pursuant to

 3
 Florida Family Law Rules of Procedure 12.491 and 12.530. The trial court
denied the motion without prejudice for failure to comply with rules 12.490
and 12.491. The trial court subsequently denied the former wife’s
amended motion for rehearing.

 The former wife then filed this appeal, challenging the trial court’s
imputation of income to her without due process and in violation of
Nadeau v. Reeves, 328 So. 3d 1001 (Fla. 4th DCA 2021), and section
61.30(2)(a)13., Florida Statutes (2025). The former wife also challenges
the trial court’s denial of her motion to vacate the final judgment without
a hearing or objection period.

 Analysis

 “The standard of review for a child support award is abuse of
discretion.” Alvarez v. Salazar, 338 So. 3d 267, 271 (Fla. 4th DCA 2022)
(quoting Smith v. Loffredo-Smith, 230 So. 3d 898, 899 (Fla. 4th DCA 2017)).
“However, the framework which a trial court has used to calculate child
support is reviewed de novo.” Varchetti, 355 So. 3d at 437 (citing Waldera
v. Waldera, 306 So. 3d 1037, 1039 (Fla. 3d DCA 2020)).

 Child support calculation is governed by Chapter 61, Florida Statutes.
Section 61.30(2) provides:

 (2) Income shall be determined on a monthly basis for each
 parent as follows:

 (a) Gross income shall include, but is not limited to, the
 following:
 ...

 13. Reimbursed expenses or in kind payments to the extent
 that they reduce living expenses.

§ 61.30(2)(a)13., Fla. Stat. (2025).

 “Under section 61.30(2)(a), a trial court’s determination of ‘income ...
on a monthly basis for each parent’ necessarily contemplates a trial court’s
initial determination of the monthly ‘gross income’ of each parent. §
61.30(2)(a), Fla. Stat. And under section 61.30(2)(a) 13., ‘[r]eimbursed
expenses or in kind payments to the extent that they reduce living
expenses’ necessarily fall within the ambit of ‘gross income.’ § 61.30(2)(a)
13., Fla. Stat.” Roman v. Roman, No. 6D2023-0841, 2026 WL 2881394,
at *3 (Fla. 6th DCA Sept. 25, 2026). “Income” is defined in sections

 4
 61.30(2)(a)1.-14. and 61.046(8), Florida Statutes (2025). Section
61.046(8) defines “income” as “any form of payment to an individual,
regardless of source, including, but not limited to: wages, salary,
commissions and bonuses, . . . and any other payments, made by any
person, private entity, federal or state government, or any unit of local
government.” § 61.046(8) (2025) (emphasis added). While both sections
specify various sources that are considered income, neither section refers
to a new spouse’s contributions.

 We have held that when a relative regularly gifts, reimburses or pays
the parent for household expenses, to the extent that the reimbursements
or payments reduce living expenses, those contributions are “income” for
child-support determinations. See Ordini v. Ordini, 701 So. 2d 663 (Fla.
4th DCA 1997) (holding that regular monthly support provided by the
husband’s parents throughout the marriage and continuing through trial
could be included in the husband’s income for purposes of determining
alimony and child support); accord Cooper v. Kahn, 696 So. 2d 1186 (Fla.
3d DCA 1997) (affirming the imputation of income based on the former
wife’s mother’s continuing and ongoing payment of the former wife’s rent,
car rental fees, and other monthly living expenses); Thalgott v. Thalgott,
571 So. 2d 1368 (Fla. 1st DCA 1990) (recognizing that the former wife’s
parents’ regular payment of household expenses—averaging
approximately $20,000 per year—was relevant to determining her income
because those payments reduced her living expenses); Garcia v. Garcia,
560 So. 2d 403 (Fla. 3d DCA 1990) (holding that, in determining income
for child-support purposes, the trial court could consider housing,
automobile, credit-card, and other expenses paid on the husband’s behalf
by his father or the family business as in-kind payments reducing his
living expenses).

 We recently held, in accord with this authority and the expansive
statutory definition of “income,” that an uncle and (new) fiancé who had
provided a former spouse “financial assistance by paying or reimbursing
her for various bills, including home utilities, car payments, auto
insurance, and groceries,” were making direct or “in-kind” payments to
her and that such payments could fairly be called “income.” Varchetti, 355
So. 3d at 435 (citing § 61.30(2)(a)13. Fla. Stat. (2021)); accord Roman, 2026
WL 2881394, at *1, 4 (boyfriend and boyfriend’s mother who resided in
marital home with former wife and paid “all the household bills, utilities,
mortgage and HOA fees” were making “in-kind” payments that counted
towards former wife’s income).

 By contrast, in Nadeau, we held that “[i]n computing a parent’s child
support obligation where that parent has remarried, it is error to use a

 5
 new spouse’s contributions to inflate the income of the remarried parent.”
Nadeau, 328 So. 3d at 1002. We rejected the trial court’s decision to count
as income the monies “her husband pays for all the expenses on her
financial affidavit.” Id. at 1001. When the new husband merely paid the
household expenses for his own household, no “payment,” in kind or
otherwise, had been made to his wife. 1

 Here, as in Nadeau, the new spouse’s payment of the mortgage and
other household expenses was not a “payment” made to the former wife.
Thus, no competent substantial evidence supports the trial court’s order
counting $8,600 of such household payments made by the new spouse as
the former wife’s “income” for child support purposes. Without a payment
(whether “in kind,” by reimbursement, otherwise) to the former wife, the
new spouse’s payments made for his own household are not the former
wife’s “income” pursuant to sections 61.30(2) or 61.046(8).

leads.caseName: Mumtaz Mf v. Sammie Lindsey and Smart Grocery, LLC
leads.text:
Cite as 2026 Ark. App. 488
 ARKANSAS COURT OF APPEALS
 DIVISION I
 No. CV-25-147

 MUMTAZ MF Opinion Delivered October 21, 2026
 APPELLANT
 APPEAL FROM THE BRADLEY
 COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT
 V. [NO. 06CV-24-35]

 SAMMIE LINDSEY AND SMART HONORABLE QUINCEY ROSS,
 GROCERY, LLC JUDGE
 APPELLEES
 AFFIRMED

 BRANDON J. HARRISON, Judge

 Ms. Mumtaz Mf appeals the Bradley County Circuit Court’s order that, after a bench

trial, awarded some $49,000 in damages for fraudulently inducing Sammie Lindsey to enter

a commercial lease. The court also denied her counterclaim for accelerated rent payments

and repairs. It awarded Lindsey attorney’s fees and denied Mumtaz’s motion to reconsider.

Here, Mumtaz argues that the judgment is undermined by legal errors. Though we agree

in part, we conclude the award is adequately supported in law and was not a clearly

erroneous determination on the facts of record. We therefore affirm.

 *

 In 2021, Lindsey and Smart Grocery, LLC sued Mumtaz in the Drew County Circuit

Court for misrepresentations of fact and breach of an implied warranty of fitness for a

particular purpose under Ark. Code Ann. § 4-2-315 (Repl. 2020). The case was transferred
 to Bradley County without objection in 2024. A bench trial was held in August 2024.

Mumtaz represented herself at trial—and not particularly assertively or well. 1 That

minimized the issues and arguments preserved for appeal, and this opinion should be read

with that in mind.

 Mumtaz owned a commercial building in Hermitage, Arkansas that she had bought

at a foreclosure sale in 2016. She said she had used the property as a grocery store and deli

with all the required licenses from the Arkansas Department of Health. She closed the store

in summer 2019 after an employee stole $7000 worth of lottery tickets. Hermitage’s mayor

reached out to Mumtaz and explained the city needed a grocery store; she was not on board.

So the mayor pivoted to Lindsey, a businessman, and asked if he would be interested in

running a grocery store. Lindsey agreed, so the mayor connected the two.

 Enter Dianeth “Dean” Mullolah, Mumtaz’s husband, who spoke with Lindsey and

ushered him around the property, the equipment, and so on. Dean explained that he and

Mumtaz had been running a grocery store and deli on the premises and that everything was

“good to go” as far as a grocer’s business was concerned. After seeing the space, hearing

that it was up to code for licensing as a grocery store, and seeing the equipment run well

enough, Lindsey signed on the dotted line. The lease agreement was for two years

beginning 1 November 2019. It required Lindsey to pay $1200 a month for rent, use the

space for retail purposes, maintain it in good condition, and pay property taxes during the

lease term.

 1
 She retained counsel later to file a motion for reconsideration and timely notices of
appeal.

 2
  Things went sour quickly. Soon after signing, Lindsey discovered that a lot of work

had to be done to open as a viable business. The biggest issue was cooling. Though the air

conditioners, coolers, and freezers worked to a degree, they could not keep things cool

enough. When Lindsey complained to Dean that the coolers weren’t working properly, he

replied, “Well, you may have done something wrong.” Lindsey paid for cleaners, had two

HVAC experts look at the equipment, and hired a plumber to install a sink and fix the drain

in the floor. Behind the cooling problem was a wiring problem. So Lindsey hired an

electrician to upgrade old and faulty wiring. Despite this work, the store failed three health

department inspections—in October 2020, November 2020, and January 2021. The

HVAC did not pass. The deli did not pass. Indeed, Lindsey testified without objection that

the health department had told Mumtaz and Dean they could never run a deli there.

 Sydney Owens, an HVAC technician Lindsey employed, couldn’t count how many

times he had come out to the store. He fixed fans that weren’t working, unclogged the

coils, drained the coils, added Freon, unstuck stuck contacts, cleaned the condensers, and

changed capacitors. Nothing made a difference. The coolers would come on, but then

stop, and wouldn’t start again. The coolers “just wasn’t really cooling,” he said. Some

condenser units simply never got power. For many of them, Owens could never find the

circuit breakers. Others had breakers that were labeled for a particular unit, but closing the

circuit wouldn’t turn the designated unit on. Eventually Owens gave up. He said, “[I]f I

see something that’s not working, . . . I’m not comfortable constantly to continue to do

work and take people[’s] money if I’m not able to fix it.” A cold statement of fact from a

warm-hearted professional.

 3
  Cooling is not a negotiable requirement for a grocery. Having concluded it would

be too costly to bring the building up to code, Lindsey contacted Dean to ask about getting

out of the lease. Twice. According to Lindsey, Dean first told him that if he would get

current with rent, Dean would let him off the contract hook. Lindsey paid his back rent—

$2,400—and assumed he was home free. Not so. Two months later, Dean asked why he

wasn’t paying rent. Lindsey explained he thought he was out of the lease. Dean said, “No,

you’re not out of the lease.” Dean had asked Mumtaz, and she vetoed the idea: “If he

agreed to the lease, he has to fulfill the lease.”

 More time passed, more rent went unpaid, and things between the parties soured

completely. By trial, Mumtaz and Dean were running the store again. But not as a grocery

store. “Just hardware.” Dean testified that when they had shut the store down in summer

2019, they had active grocery and deli licenses and were operating the store as both.

Department of health records would confirm that, he said.

 From then until Lindsey leased the property, Dean would come in two or three times

a week and run the cooler for an hour, “two hours sometimes,” to make sure it was cooling

enough. He said the HVAC system “need[s] maintenance all the time.” Sometimes the

Freon is low, or the capacitor goes, or the breaker trips; those are “the problems we have

that are commonplace.”

 When he and Mumtaz took over after the lease term, they had to spend a lot of

money getting the (hardware) store ready. Why? The air conditioning “was not working

in good condition at that time.” Dean didn’t know what all was done, but “a lot of air

 4
 condition people came and, you know, did it.” One of them told him a compressor had to

be changed, and another was in bad condition.

 Mumtaz testified that she had a grocery license from the day she bought the building

until she leased it to Lindsey. Inspectors came every six months. She had two or three total

violations in that time. Most were “small things, like the soap or the towels or the

refrigeration was not cooling enough.” When she had bought the building, the HVAC was

not working. An HVAC technician told her the air conditioning had died. She spent

$8,000 to resurrect it. How many times had she needed to fix it since? “Oh, many times.”

“Many time[s],” she repeated. “Like, the air condition[ing] units all the time.” She had

been to a safety course and knew what temperatures the coolers and freezers needed to stay

under. Whenever the HVAC needed maintenance or repair she called a technician because

“we need to do it to keep the product good.” The last day they were in business, the

temperatures were where they were supposed to be.

 After Lindsey vacated the building, the store was not used for two years. In that

time, Mumtaz said, rats gnawed through a lot of the electric wires. As a landlord, she had

wanted two things from Lindsey. “I wanted to rent that building. . . . And I wanted them

to maintain that building.” She agreed that she had wanted to incentivize a lease. Mumtaz

admitted that she told Lindsey before he signed the lease that, though the building was now

closed, she and Dean had recently been operating a grocery store, deli, and hardware store

there. But she “didn’t say that [would] work. I said we did it. I said we did it.” Her word,

she said, “is in that [lease] agreement. Okay? I go by the agreement.” And the lease

 5
 agreement said the property was leased as is, and that it was the lessee’s duty to maintain the

building and cooling system.

 But Mumtaz was not the only one who had spoken to Lindsey. Dean had too. And

Mumtaz acknowledged he was authorized to speak for her on some matters and had told

Lindsey, “[W]e have a deli license. We have a grocery license. You’re good to go.”

Sammie’s wife Catherine confirmed that Mumtaz was present when Dean had made those

statements. Though Mumtaz denied Dean had authority to speak for her on all matters

(“[h]e’s not authorized to say anything I did not say”), she could not say how Lindsey was

supposed to tell the difference. And that apparently made a difference.

 After closing arguments, the circuit court addressed Mumtaz:

 THE COURT: . . . At this point in time, I will leave evidence open for the
 licenses. Okay? I want to see those three licenses you said you
 were carrying on this building. All right? I also want to see what
 infractions you carried on those for the deli, for the grocery side
 and any other licenses you had from the health department.
 . . . I’m only worried about this building in Hermitage. I
 don’t care about the one in Strong.

 MUMTAZ: Oh. Okay. I have them.

(Emphasis added.)

 She did not have them. In a letter dated 1 August 2024, she attached tax bills and

other records the court had invited her to submit. But no licenses or violation notices, past

or present, were produced. Mumtaz represented that she had called the health department,

and an employee told her the license was closed in 2019 and not active now, so they could

not be printed. Lindsey’s own supplement includes this 13 August 2024 Freedom of

Information Act request from his counsel:

 6
  I am interested in any and all records of the Arkansas Department of Health
 regarding any businesses or interaction with the [Department] regarding a
 commercial property situated at 112 W. 3rd St. in Hermitage, Arkansas.

 I hereby request a copy of all licenses, applications, inspections, notices,
 suspensions, revocations, or any and all other communications regarding
 commercial activity at that location. This would include any property
 operated by Mumtaz MF, Dollar Saver Market, Inc., Smart Grocery, LLC,
 Sammie Lindsey, or any other party.

But the record does not indicate what, if anything, came in response.

 On November 7, about three months later, the circuit court ruled in Lindsey’s favor

and awarded him $48,910.75 in damages and attorney’s fees in an amount to be determined

(eventually $4,895 plus court costs). Because Lindsey was an experienced business owner

and the court found he had failed to perform some due diligence before signing the lease, it

assigned him some responsibility for the commercial mess. To adjust for Lindsey’s oversight,

the court subtracted three months’ rent ($3600) from the award above. All Mumtaz’s

counterclaims were denied. 2

 November 22, through newly acquired attorneys, she moved for reconsideration or,

alternatively, to set aside judgment. The circuit court expressly denied the motion

December 10. She timely appealed the November 7 and December 10 orders. We ordered

her to file a replacement for her principal brief because of deficiencies. Mf v. Lindsey, 2026

Ark. App. 214. Two judges now reach the merits; the third would dismiss for a recurring

briefing deficiency. The judgment will be affirmed nonetheless, as now detailed.

 2
 Mumtaz does not raise any issue on appeal about the denial of her counterclaims, so
we discuss them no further.

 7
  The circuit court grounded its award in both the fraudulent-inducement and

implied-warranty-of-fitness theories Lindsey pleaded. Mumta

leads.caseName: Sca Management, LLC v. Ann Donovan, P.A.
leads.text:
Cite as 2026 Ark. App. 494
 ARKANSAS COURT OF APPEALS
 DIVISION II
 No. CV-25-181

 SCA MANAGEMENT, LLC
 Opinion Delivered October 21, 2026

 APPELLANT
 APPEAL FROM THE BENTON
 COUNTY CIRCUIT COURT
 V. [NO. 04CV-24-852]

 ANN DONOVAN, P.A.; ANN HONORABLE GARY ARNOLD,
 DONOVAN; AND ALL OTHER JUDGE
 OCCUPANTS OF 700 N 13TH ST A,
 ROGERS, AR 72756
 APPELLEES DISMISSED WITHOUT PREJUDICE

 WENDY SCHOLTENS WOOD, Judge

 Appellant SCA Management, LLC (“SCA”), appeals from an order of the Benton

County Circuit Court granting the motion of appellees Ann Donovan, P.A., and Ann

Donovan (collectively referred to as “Donovan”) to set aside the circuit court’s grant of

summary judgment in favor of SCA. We dismiss the appeal without prejudice for lack of a

final order.

 On March 21, 2024, SCA filed a complaint for unlawful detainer seeking damages in

connection with a commercial property owned by SCA where Donovan leased office space

for a law firm. The complaint alleged that Donovan had failed to pay rent and costs in the

amount of $17,963.59 and refused to vacate after written and lawful demand. SCA attached

to the complaint a written lease agreement dated October 8, 2015, between the Schmieding
 Foundation, Inc., as lessor, and Ann Donovan, P.A., as lessee, for 700 N. 13th Street, Suite

A. The lease agreement was for a term of twenty-four months, from November 1, 2015 to

October 31, 2017, with a rental rate of $1260 a month, subject to a late-payment penalty of

5 percent.

 Donovan answered the complaint and filed a counterclaim for damages, a statutory

penalty, and attorney’s fees. Donovan’s counterclaim alleged, among other things, that the

written lease agreement with a previous landlord had expired in 2017, a new agreement had

not been executed, and SCA owed Donovan for expenses incurred in connection with the

property, including expenses relating to a nonfunctioning heating and air unit that was never

repaired.

 SCA moved for summary judgment on July 12, 2024. Thirty-two days later, SCA’s

attorney filed an “Affidavit of Service of Motion” averring that a file-stamped copy of the

motion for summary judgment was served on Donovan on July 18 via USPS Priority Mail.

Copies of the envelope from the mailing and a USPS tracking update were submitted with

the affidavit. SCA’s attorney informed the circuit court by letter dated August 14 that

Donovan was served with the summary-judgment motion but did not file a timely response

and therefore had failed to “meet proof with proof” to refute SCA’s claims.

 On August 16, the circuit court entered an order granting SCA’s motion for summary

judgment, finding that “the failure to file any response by [Donovan] lacks any proof to

oppose the claims for damages set forth by [SCA].” The court also dismissed Donovan’s

counterclaim because “judgment has been rendered against [Donovan] on all of the claims

 2
 made in the verified Complaint.” The court awarded SCA judgment against Donovan in the

amount $27,843.52, plus $3,780.00 “for violations of Ark. Code Ann. [§] 18-60-309(b)” and

attorney’s fees in the amount of $4,000.00.

 On September 30, Donovan moved to stay execution of judgment and simultaneously

moved to have the judgment set aside pursuant to Rule 60 of the Arkansas Rules of Civil

Procedure.1 Donovan claimed that they had not been served with the motion for summary

judgment and had only recently learned of the circuit court’s August 16 order granting

summary judgment. Donovan urged the circuit court to set aside its judgment under Rule

60(a) to “correct errors or mistakes or to prevent the miscarriage of justice” because they had

“valid defenses” that were not considered on summary judgment. SCA moved to strike

Donovan’s Rule 60 motion, and the circuit court held a hearing on both motions on

November 8.

 On November 14, the circuit court entered an order denying SCA’s motion to strike

and granting Donovan’s motion to set aside the August 16 summary-judgment order. The

court found that Donovan had not been sufficiently served with the motion for summary

judgment and that the motion “failed to address all allegations and the supporting exhibits

 1
 Arkansas Rule of Civil Procedure 60(a) provides: “To correct errors or mistakes or
to prevent the miscarriage of justice, the court may modify or vacate a judgment, order or
decree on motion of the court or any party, with prior notice to all parties, within ninety
days of its having been filed with the clerk.”

 3
 in [Donovan’s] Answer and Counterclaim and left genuine issues of material facts to be

decided.”2

 On November 25, SCA filed a Rule 60 motion to vacate, alter, and amend the circuit

court’s November 14 order setting aside its August 16 summary-judgment order. That

motion was deemed denied by operation of law after thirty days.

 On December 26, SCA filed a notice purporting to appeal the circuit court’s

November 14 order setting aside the August 16 order of summary judgment and the deemed

denial of SCA’s post judgment motion seeking relief from the November 14 order under

Rule 60. However, we cannot address the merits of the appeal because SCA has appealed a

nonfinal order.

 Rule 2(a)(1) of the Arkansas Rules of Appellate Procedure–Civil provides that an

appeal may be taken from a final judgment or decree entered by a circuit court. The finality

of a circuit court’s judgment or decree is a jurisdictional requirement, and its purpose is to

avoid piecemeal litigation. See Eldridge v. Waugh, 2022 Ark. App. 241, at 4; see also Lamb v.

JFM, Inc., 311 Ark. 89, 91, 842 S.W.2d 10, 11 (1992). To be final and appealable, an order

must dismiss the parties from the court, discharge them from the action, or conclude their

rights to the subject matter in controversy. Barton v. Brockington, 2016 Ark. App. 138, at 3,

 2
 In Sellers v. Felton, this court recited the following well-established principles: “When
the proof supporting a motion for summary judgment is insufficient, there is no duty on the
part of the opposing party to meet proof with proof. Summary judgment is not granted
simply because the opposing party fails to respond to the motion.” 2021 Ark. App. 247, at
3, 626 S.W.3d 121, 123 (internal citations omitted).

 4
 487 S.W.3d 820, 822. A judgment or decree that contemplates further judicial action is not

final. Eldridge, 2022 Ark. App. 241, at 4.

 Here, the only final order was the August 16 order granting summary judgment

against Donovan. However, that is not the order on appeal. The order on appeal is the circuit

court’s November 14 order that expressly set aside the August 16 summary-judgment order

pursuant to Ark. R. Civ. P. 60(a).

 It is well established that an order denying a motion for summary judgment is not a

final, appealable order. Eldridge, 2022 Ark. App. 241, at 6. We also have held that a circuit

court’s order setting aside its prior order of summary judgment within ninety days is not an

appealable order because it is not a final order dismissing the parties from the action. 3 See id.

at 6–7; see also Lamb, 311 Ark. at 92, 842 S.W.2d at 12 (explaining that if the appellate court

considers such an appeal and affirms the order vacating the judgment, then the case would

be tried, the lower court’s rulings at trial would be subject to appeal, and the case could be

appealed a second time resulting in two appeals when one would suffice).

 3
 Our appellate courts have held that an order vacating a judgment after ninety days,
on the other hand, is an appealable order because it determines the outcome in the
equivalent of an independent action to set aside a judgment. See Lamb, 311 Ark. at 92, 842
S.W.2d at 11 (noting that in such an independent action, the judgment creditor could lose
his established creditor’s rights); see also Cigna Ins. Co. v. Brisson, 294 Ark. 504, 506-A, 746
S.W.2d 558 (1988) (supplemental opinion on grant of rehearing) (holding that an order
setting aside a prior order and reinstating an action entered more than ninety days after an
earlier order it purported to modify or vacate was appealable even though it did not dispose
of the action); see also Eldridge, 2022 Ark. App. 241, at 6 (distinguishing Citibank, N.A. v.
Carruth, 2015 Ark. App. 704).

 5
  On November 14, the circuit court entered an order that set aside its August 16

summary-judgment order within the ninety-day period. See Ark. R. Civ. P. 60. The November

14 order vacating the summary judgment does not dismiss or discharge the parties from the

court, nor does it conclude their rights to the subject matter in controversy. Rather, it “places

both of the parties back in the position they were in before the judgment was entered, and

it is clear that neither party had a right to appeal before the judgment was entered.” Lamb,

311 Ark. at 91, 842 S.W.2d at 11 (internal citations omitted). Therefore, the November 14

order is not a final and appealable order, and we are without jurisdiction to review it. 4

 Because SCA’s Rule 60 motion sought relief from a nonfinal order, the filing of the

Rule 60 motion did not make the November 14 order appealable; therefore, we lack

jurisdiction to review the deemed denial of that motion as well. See Simshauser v. Simshauser,

 4
 We note that SCA’s jurisdictional statement cites for purposes of appellate
jurisdiction Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(a)(3) (permitting appeal from an order that grants or
refuses a new trial); Ark. R. App. P.–Civ. 2(a)(4) (permitting appeal from an order that strikes
out answer, or any part of answer, or any pleading in an action); and Ark. R. App. P.–Civ.
2(a)(5) (permitting appeal from an order that vacates or sustains an attachment or
garnishment). None of these applies in SCA’s case. Our supreme court has said that, if after
“a complete adversarial proceeding,” a circuit court grants a new trial under Rule 59 of the
Arkansas Rules of Civil Procedure, the order granting a new trial is appealable under Rule
2(a)(3). Lamb, 311 Ark. at 93, 842 S.W.2d at 12. Our rules of appellate procedure, however,
do not provide such a right of appeal when, as in this case, “a judgment is obtained after less
than a complete adversarial proceeding and is vacated within ninety days under Rule 60 even
though, at the least, a partial new trial will be the result.” Id., 842 S.W.2d at 12. The circuit
court’s order vacating its August 16 summary-judgment order, moreover, does not strike out
an answer, any part of an answer, or any pleading; and it does not vacate an attachment or
garnishment.

 6
 2026 Ark. App. 191, at 8, 731 S.W.3d 849, 855–56. Accordingly, we dismiss the appeal

without prejudice.

 Dismissed without prejudice.

 TUCKER and HIXSON, JJ., agree.

 The Overton Firm, LLC, by: J. Don Overton, for appellant.

 One brief only.

 7

leads.caseName: 513 W. 26th Realty LLC v. George Billis Galleries, Inc.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
513 W. 26th Realty LLC v George Billis Galleries, Inc. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06058 
 October 20, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Rosado, J. 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 513 West 26th Realty LLC, Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 George Billis Galleries, Inc. et al., Defendants-Appellants. 

 Supreme Court, Appellate Division, First Judicial Department 
 Decided and Entered: October 20, 2026 
 Index No. 160266/20|Appeal No. 5735|Case No. 2025-00996| 
 Peter H. Moulton 
 David Friedman John R. Higgitt Llinét M. Rosado Kelly O'Neill Levy 

 James G. Marsh, P.C., Mineola (James G. Marsh of counsel), for George Billis Galleries, Inc., and George Billis, appellants. 
 Muriel Goode-Trufant, Corporation Counsel, New York (Jamison Davies, Richard Dearing and Devin Slack of counsel), for City of New York, appellant. 
 Smith & Shapiro, New York (Harry Shapiro of counsel), for respondent.

 Defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, New York County (Paul A. Goetz, J.), entered on or about December 31, 2024, which declared that New York City Administrative Code § 22-1005 violates the Contracts Clause of article I, section 10 of the United States Constitution, reinstated plaintiff 513 West 26th Realty, LLC's second and third causes of action against defendant George Billis, and denied defendants George Billis and the City of New York's respective motions to dismiss the complaint.

Rosado, J.
 [*1] 
 This case calls on us to determine the constitutionality of New York City Administrative Code § 22-1005, commonly referred to as the "guaranty law." Enacted by the New York City Council in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, the guaranty law precluded the enforcement of personal liability guaranties of certain commercial leases for a statutorily prescribed 16-month period. Principally, we are asked to decide whether this law, which the City Council passed as a means of mitigating the economic fallout of the public health crisis and to help small business owners avoid personal bankruptcy, impermissibly impairs existing contractual obligations in violation of the Contracts Clause of article I, section 10 of the United States Constitution. For the reasons that follow, we conclude that the guaranty law does not violate the Contracts Clause. In doing so, we make no judgment as to the wisdom of the guaranty law; rather, applying the principles applicable to any Contracts Clause challenge, we find that the law passes constitutional muster. 
 Introduction 
 In this commercial guaranty action, plaintiff-landlord 513 West 26th Realty, LLC (the landlord) alleges that defendant-tenant George Billis Galleries, Inc. (the tenant), which operates an art exhibition space, breached its lease with the landlord and that defendant-guarantor George Billis (the guarantor) breached his guaranty after the tenant failed to make rent payments during the pandemic. Supreme Court initially granted partial summary judgment to the guarantor, dismissing the causes of action as against him as barred by the guaranty law. This Court reversed and remanded the case ( 513 W. 26th Realty LLC v George Billis Galleries, Inc. , 220 AD3d 525, 525-526 [1st Dept 2023]), to allow the record to be further developed and a determination made as to the law's constitutionality in light of the Southern District of New York's decision in Melendez v City of New York (668 F Supp 3d 184 [SD NY 2023], vacated and remanded for dismissal by Bochner v City of New York , 118 F4th 505 [2d Cir 2024]) (hereinafter Melendez III ). Before it was vacated, the Southern District's decision found the guaranty law violated the Contracts Clause. Our decision also directed plaintiff to serve notice on the City of New York to allow it to intervene as a defendant ( id. ). 
 The tenant, the guarantor, and the City now appeal from the decision of Supreme Court after this Court's remand. In light of Melendez III and in consideration of concerns about the guaranty law raised by the Second Circuit in Melendez v City of New York (16 F4th 992 [2d Cir 2021]), Supreme Court declared that the law violates the Contracts Clause, reinstated the causes of action as against the guarantor, and denied defendants' respective motions to dismiss. 
 [*2] 
 With a sufficiently developed record now before us and only pure questions of law left to resolve, we hold that when analyzing the instant Contracts Clause challenge under the three-part test articulated by the United States Supreme Court ( see Energy Reserves Group, Inc. v Kansas Power & Light Co. , 459 US 400, 411-413 [1983]), the guaranty law is constitutional. Accordingly, we reverse Supreme Court's decision. We reach this determination in view of "the strong presumption of constitutionality that attaches to every statute" ( Local Govt. Assistance Corp. v Sales Tax Asset Receivable Corp. , 2 NY3d 524, 535 [2004]) and the substantial deference owed to the City Council's legislative judgment ( see Keystone Bituminous Coal Assn. v DeBenedictis , 480 US 470, 505 [1987] ["unless the State is itself a contracting party, courts should properly defer to legislative judgment as to the necessity and reasonableness of a particular measure"] [internal quotation marks omitted], quoting Energy Reserves , 459 US at 413; Buffalo Teachers Fedn. v Tobe , 464 F3d 362, 369 [2d Cir 2006] [same], cert denied 550 US 918 [2007]). Such deference is particularly appropriate in light of the declared emergency in New York State at the time the law was enacted ( see United States Trust Co. of New York v New Jersey , 431 US 1, 22 n 19 [1977]; Home Bldg. & Loan Assn. v Blaisdell (290 US 398, 426 [1934]; Buffalo Teachers Fedn. , 464 F3d at 373). 
 Factual and Procedural History 
 The COVID-19 Pandemic and Economic Fallout 
 On January 31, 2020, the federal government declared a public health emergency to assist the country's health care community in responding to COVID-19. On March 7, 2020, the Governor, empowered by the New York State Legislature's amendment of Executive Law § 29-a to authorize him to issue any directive necessary to cope with a state disaster emergency (2020 McKinney's Sess Law News of NY [L 2020, ch 23, § 2]), declared such an emergency in response to the growing threat that the virus posed to New York State (Executive Order [A. Cuomo] No. 202 [9 NYCRR 8.202]). The Governor enacted stringent emergency measures, including, among others, a series of executive orders banning events and gatherings of more than 50 people, prohibiting restaurants and bars from serving patrons on their premises, and directing the closure of all nonessential retail establishments and businesses, as well as personal care services, such as barbershops, hair salons, and tattoo parlors (Executive Order [A. Cuomo] Nos. 202.3 [9 NYCRR 8.202.3]; 202.6 [9 NYCRR 8.202.6]; and 202.7 [9 NYCRR 8.202.7]). 
 [*3] 
 Although such measures were viewed as necessary to combat the spread of the virus, they were also expected to have a profound economic impact on the City, in particular to its small businesses. On March 16, 2020, bracing for the economic fallout of the public health crisis, the City Comptroller conservatively estimated that the City could lose $3.2 billion in tax revenue from downturns in the entertainment, hotel, real estate, restaurant, retail, travel, and tourism sectors over the next six months ( Comptroller Stringer: City Must Take Immediate Action to Prepare For Economic Impacts of COVID-19 and Protect Vital Services for Most Vulnerable New Yorkers , Office of the New York City Comptroller [Press Release, Mar. 16, 2020], available at https://comptroller.nyc.gov/newsroom/comptroller-stringer-city-must-take-immediate-action-to-prepare-for-economic-impacts-of-covid-19-and-protect-vital-services-for-most-vulnerable-new-yorkers [last accessed May 8, 2026]). He warned of "significant projected losses," with restaurant sales estimated to plummet by 80% and real estate and retail sales by 20% ( id. ). A prolonged recession was anticipated ( id. ). 
 In the following weeks and months, the economic devastation of the pandemic on the City and State became clear. Nearly 144,000 unemployment claims were filed in the City during the week of March 22, 2020, an increase of 2,637% from the year before (Corina Knoll et al., 11 Numbers That Show How the Coronavirus Has Changed N.Y.C. , NY Times, Apr. 20, 2020, updated Mar. 27, 2024, available at https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/20/nyregion/coronavirus-nyc-numbers-unemployment.html [last accessed May 8, 2026]). According to an April 29, 2020 report (the April 29 report) of the City Council Committee on Consumer Affairs and Business Licensing and Committee on Small Business, entitled, "OVERSIGHT: The Impact of COVID-19 on Small Businesses in New York City," sales for the State's restaurant industry alone were estimated to have declined by 79% by April 2020. A loss of $3.6 billion in sales revenue was forecast for just that month, and 80% of workers were reported to have lost their jobs, the April 29 report noted, citing an April 2020 survey conducted by the New York State Restaurant Association. Close to 10 months into the pandemic, citywide unemployment remained at 12% (Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York City Economic Indicators [Mar. 13, 2021], cached at https://perma.cc/Q9NU-W3QJ, formerly available at https://www.newyorkfed.org/ 
 medialibrary/media/research/regional_economy/charts/Regional_NYC). The result was that many of the smaller businesses contributing to the City's inimitable character could not operate, or could not operate in a manner permitting them to generate the income they relied on to pay their formidable rent costs, leading to rampant lease defaults and the threatened closures of these businesses. 
 The Guaranty Law 
 [*4] 
 Amidst the twin public health and economic crises, the City Council on April 22, 2020 introduced a package of 13 bills "to help small businesses in the City weather the negative impacts of the COVID-19 outbreak" (April 29 report at 5). The legislative package included Int. No. 1932, the early version of the guaranty law, which, as proposed, would have barred the enforcement of personal guaranties against commercial tenants "impacted by COVID-19" for defaults occurring during the "COVID-19 period." FN1 City Council Member Carlina Rivera, a cosponsor of the bill, stated it would "ensure city business owners don't face the loss of their businesses and personal financial ruin or bankruptcy as a result of this state of emergency" (Transcript of Proceedings, Stated Meeting of the New York City Council [Apr. 22, 2020]). She further noted that small businesses were "closing and losing weeks of income through no fault of their own and allowing small business owners to keep their spaces will be integral to the city's ability to recovery after the virus" ( id. ). 
 In the period leading up to the guaranty law's enactment, the City Council issued the April 29 report detailing the impact of the pandemic on small businesses in the City and State. The report cited, among a multitude of sources, the March 16, 2020 City Comptroller press release, an April 2020 New York State Restaurant Association survey, and an April 2020 National Bureau of Economic Research survey finding that the current and expected impacts of the pandemic on small businesses were "particularly sharp" in the Mid-Atlantic region, with 54% of small businesses in the region reportedly closing due to COVID-19 and employment falling by an average of 47% (Alexander W. Bartik et al., How Are Small Businesses Adjusting to COVID-19? Early Evidence from a Survey , National Bureau of Economic Research, available at https://www.nber.org/ 
 system/files/working_papers/w26989/w26989.pdf [last accessed May 8, 2026]). 
 [*5] 
 The April 29 report also discussed the Fede

leads.caseName: Mark Matthews, V. City Of Tacoma
