NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has 
not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION SEVEN 

THE WAFFLE, LLC, 

 Plaintiff and Appellant, 

 v. 

TUCKER INVESTMENT 
GROUP, LLC et al. 

 Defendants and 
Respondents. 

 B341347 

(Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. SC129215) 

 APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of 
Los Angeles County, Mark H. Epstein, Judge. Affirmed. 
 Ellis George, Eric M. George and Serli Polatoglu for 
Plaintiff and Appellant. 
 Saul Ewing, William E. Adams and Matthew A. Young for 
Defendants and Respondents. 
__________________________ 

2 
The Waffle, LLC appeals from a judgment in favor of 
William Tucker and Tucker Investment Group, LLC (TIG; 
collectively, the Tucker defendants) after the trial court granted 
the Tucker defendants’ motion to confirm an arbitration award in 
their favor and denied The Waffle’s motion to vacate the award. 
The Waffle contends the trial court erred because the arbitrator 
exceeded the scope of his authority by relying on findings made 
by the court in phase I of a trial on related issues; failed to issue 
a “reasoned award” that addressed the principal argument raised 
by The Waffle; and erred in awarding attorneys’ fees for work 
performed on behalf of defendants who had settled. We affirm. 

FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 

A. The Restaurant Lease and Notice of Breach 
Tucker is the managing member of TIG. In 2014 TIG 
signed a 10-year master lease under which it leased a commercial 
property in Westwood, Los Angeles (the premises). In 2016 or 
2017 Tucker and The Waffle began negotiating a potential 
sublease of the premises with The Waffle’s principal, Gavin 
Polone. The Waffle had an existing restaurant in Hollywood and 
sought to open a second location in Westwood. On March 30, 
2017 TIG and The Waffle entered a 10-year lease for a restaurant 
space on the premises (the lease). Under an addendum to the 
lease and an attached construction work letter, TIG agreed to 
provide a “4-inch grease waste line connected to a 3000 gallon 
grease interceptor in compliance with code” (the interceptor). 
The lease did not contain a deadline to install the interceptor or 
require installation before TIG delivered possession of the 
premises to The Waffle. 

3 
Instead, the lease contained a cure provision that provided 
time limits for performance of TIG’s obligations under the lease 
upon a claimed breach by The Waffle. Section 13.6, 
subsection (a), provided: “Lessor shall not be deemed in breach of 
this Lease unless Lessor fails within a reasonable time to 
perform an obligation required to be performed by 
Lessor. . . . [A] reasonable time shall in no event be less than 
30 days after receipt by Lessor . . . of written notice specifying 
wherein such obligation of Lessor has not been performed; 
provided, however, that if the nature of Lessor’s obligation is 
such that more than 30 days are reasonably required for its 
performance, then Lessor shall not be in breach if performance is 
commenced within such 30 day period and thereafter diligently 
pursued to completion.” Section 31 of the lease provided 
attorneys’ fees to the prevailing party in any action or proceeding 
involving the premises. 
After the parties signed the lease, TIG’s project manager, 
Johnnie Morgan of Coastline Construction Management, Inc. 
(collectively, the Coastline defendants), started to analyze the 
feasibility of installing the interceptor in an elevated area behind 
the premises. From late 2017 to early 2018, TIG, Tucker, 
Morgan, Polone, The Waffle’s architect, and The Waffle’s 
mechanical and plumbing engineer discussed the feasibility of 
installing the interceptor at the premises. The viability of the 
installation was impacted by the interceptor’s large size, location 
(which required excavation of the slope behind the premises), and 
installation costs. Morgan also reached out to the City of Los 
Angeles Sanitation and Environment Department to discuss the 
interceptor, and he arranged a site visit by the City. Given the 
challenges to install the interceptor, the parties discussed as an 

4 
alternative a Schier grease trap (the Schier). The Waffle 
remained skeptical that the Schier was an acceptable alternative. 
On December 11, 2017 Morgan emailed The Waffle’s 
architect with plumbing plans that included the Schier instead of 
the interceptor. Tucker and Polone continued to discuss the 
Schier as an alternative to the interceptor. Polone expressed 
skepticism that the Schier would work given the amount of 
grease the restaurant would produce, and Tucker explained that 
the Schier was feasible and would not pose the same challenges 
as the interceptor. On February 15, 2018 Polone emailed Tucker 
that he had “‘no reason to think your proposal for substituting 
the [interceptor] called for in our agreement for the Schier unit 
will be acceptable.’” Tucker responded on February 17, “‘I don’t 
understand why you are not open to being cooperative and 
reasonable . . . . [Y]ou seem to say that you now won’t work with 
us even if [the Schier] is shown to be a great option.’” On 
March 9 Polone emailed Tucker, “‘[W]e must resolve the issues 
with the . . . grease interceptor.’” 
On March 19, 2018 The Waffle sent Tucker a letter (the 
notice) providing “notice of your breach of our March 30, 2017 
Lease.” The notice cited the requirement in the lease to provide 
the interceptor and explained The Waffle refused to sign off on 
the plans for the premises because the Tucker defendants did 
“not provide for the required 3,000 gallon grease [interceptor].” 
The notice concluded, “We ask that you instead provide plans 
consistent with the [construction] [w]ork [l]etter and the Lease, 
and because to date you have failed to do so, we are providing 
this notice per Section 13.6(a) of our Lease.” The next day Tucker 
sent Polone a letter to confirm receipt of the notice, in which he 
explained that TIG had not inserted the Schier into the plans. 

5 
Tucker added, “‘[W]e understood you had reserved your rights 
with respect to the grease interceptor to be installed. We were 
simply request[ing] [the plans] be initialed’” per the terms of the 
lease. 
After further discussions, on April 6, 2018 Polone emailed 
Tucker to decline the Schier as an alternative, stating, “As I have 
said many times, I did not think this substitution would be 
acceptable and this decision is now final.” Tucker responded, 
“FYI, I’m now going back to engineers about installing the 3,000-
gallon [interceptor].” Tucker then spoke with both a plumbing 
engineer and a civil engineer about the interceptor. On April 16 
Tucker emailed Polone to state he was “‘interviewing shoring 
engineers for the design work of both the [interceptor] and the 
structural impact on the building. Will keep you posted when we 
know more about the timeline.’” 

B. The Lawsuit and Stipulation To Bifurcate Trial 
On May 2, 2018 The Waffle filed a lawsuit against the 
Tucker and Coastline defendants. The operative third amended 
complaint alleged causes of action against the Tucker and 
Coastline defendants for fraud and negligent misrepresentation 
and against TIG for rescission, breach of written contract, and 
declaratory relief. The Waffle alleged with respect to the fraud 
and negligent misrepresentation causes of action that the 
defendants acted fraudulently before and after executing the 
lease, made false promises, and concealed and misrepresented 
key issues relating to the grease interceptor.1 On 

1 TIG subsequently filed a cross-complaint against The 
Waffle for breach of the lease and related causes of action, which 
it later voluntarily dismissed. 

6 
November 16, 2021 the parties stipulated to bifurcate the trial, 
with a bench trial on the breach of contract cause of action 
against TIG (phase I) and a subsequent jury trial on the 
remaining causes of action against the Tucker and Coastline 
defendants (phase II). 

C. Phase I: The Bench Trial on the Breach of Contract Cause of 
Action 
In November 2021 the trial court held a six-day bench trial 
on The Waffle’s breach of contract cause of action against TIG. 
On December 6, 2021 the court orally announced its ruling. The 
court explained that under the “odd” language in section 13.6, 
subsection (a), of the lease, “even if there is a clear failure by the 
landlord to perform an unambiguous requirement in the contract 
that the landlord is required to do, it is still not a breach . . . until 
the tenant gives the landlord notice, specifies the duty that the 
landlord has not yet performed, and 30 days has expired subject 
to the [condition allowing for additional time if the duty cannot 
be cured in 30 days].” Under the lease, therefore, the landlord is 
not in breach unless “it is not finished within 30 days,” or, if the 
duty cannot be reasonably completed in 30 days, “it is not 
commenced within 30 days and thereafter diligently pursued.” 
Because installation of the interceptor “was not a 30-day cure,” 
TIG “need[ed] to commence [installation] within 30 days and 
diligently proceed thereafter to completion.” The court explained 
Tucker “did do something. He did start. He did say, ‘I will talk 
to the engineers,’ and he did talk to his team. He did talk to 
Mr. Morgan. And he did say, ‘Okay. We are going to have to go 
with the 3,000-gallon grease interceptor.’” Tucker “had given up 
on the Schier grease [interceptor] . . . and had instructed 

7 
Mr. Morgan to move forward with putting in the 3,000-gallon 
grease interceptor.” The court found TIG did not breach the lease 
and ruled in favor of TIG on the breach of contract cause of 
action. 

D. Phase II: The Jury Trial on the Remaining Causes of 
Action 
In March and April 2022, the trial court held a jury trial on 
The Waffle’s fraud and negligent misrepresentation causes of 
action against the Tucker and Coastline defendants. During the 
trial the parties presented their arguments; called witnesses, 
including experts; and presented documentary evidence of the 
parties’ communications. The court excluded any mention of the 
disposition of phase I of the trial. On April 4, 2022 the jury 
returned a verdict for the Coastline defendants on The Waffle’s 
negligent misrepresentation claim but was deadlocked on the 
remaining causes of action against the Tucker defendants (for 
fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation) and the Coastline 
defendants (for fraudulent misrepresentation), resulting in a 
mistrial. Instead of retrying the remaining causes of action 
against the Tucker and Coastline defendants, the parties agreed 
to arbitrate the claims. 

E. The Stipulation To Arbitrate 
On June 28, 2022 the parties signed a stipulation agreeing 
to “submit all remaining claims and issues (including any 
motions for attorney fees) in the above-captioned litigation to 
private binding arbitration.” The stipulation directed the 
arbitrator to apply the substantive law of California on the 
merits and “follow the procedural rules of ADR Services, Inc.” 

8 
The parties agreed to “waive any right to appeal the decisions 
made during the action, and further agree[d] to be bound by the 
determination of the arbitrator absent evidence of any activities 
described in California Code of Civil Procedure Section 1286.2.”2 
The stipulation “permitted” and “encouraged” the “use as 
evidence during arbitration the written discovery, documents, 
deposition transcripts and trial transcripts exchanged and 
prepared during the action” and “deemed admitted for purposes 
of arbitration

leads.text:
[Cite as U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v. Shaffer, 2026-Ohio-4102.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
ELEVENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
GEAUGA COUNTY 

U.S. BANK NATIONAL 
ASSOCIATION, NOT IN ITS 
INDIVIDUAL CAPACITY BUT 
SOLELY AS TRUSTEE OF NRZ 
PASS-THROUGH TRUST XI, 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, 

 - vs - 

THERESA A. SHAFFER a.k.a. 
THERESA A. MCFAUL-SHAFFER 
a.k.a. THERESA MCFAUL SHAFFER, 
et al., 

 Defendant-Appellant. 
CASE NO. 2025-G-0031 

Civil Appeal from the 
Court of Common Pleas 

Trial Court No. 2024 F 000399 

MEMORANDUM OPINION AND JUDGMENT ENTRY 

Decided: October 19, 2026 
Judgment: Appeal dismissed 

Suzanne M. Godenswager , and David T. Brady , Sandhu Law Group, L.L.C., 1213 
Prospect Avenue, Suite 300, Cleveland, OH 44115 (For Plaintiff-Appellee). 

Andrew M. Engel , Whitney E. Kaster , and Marc E. Dann , Dann Law, 15000 Madison 
Avenue, Lakewood, OH 44107 (For Defendant-Appellant). 

ROBERT J. PATTON, J. 
{¶1} Defendant-appellant, Theresa A. Shaffer (“Shaffer”), appeals from the trial 
court’s decision granting plaintiff -appellee, U.S. Bank National Association ’s, as trustee 
of NRZ Pass-Through Trust XI (“U.S. Bank National”), motion for summary judgment on 
its complaint for foreclosure. 

PAGE 2 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
{¶2} Upon review, we conclude that the trial court’s judgment and decree of 
foreclosure is not a final appealable order. The appeal is dismissed. 
Substantive and Procedural Facts 
{¶3} On June 12, 2024, U.S. Bank National filed a Complaint for money, 
foreclosure, and other equitable relief against Shaffer, Brian Shaffer (“Brian”), and their 
unknown spouses .1 The complaint also named Capital One National Association, The 
Huntington National Bank, LCE Federal Credit Union, John Carro ll University, and the 
Geauga County Treasurer. According to the complaint, Shaffer owed U.S. Bank National 
$142,118.85 on the note and mortgage with interest at the annual rate of 6.65% from 
March 1, 2018. 
{¶4} John Carroll University filed its answer on July 8, 2024. LCE Federal Credit 
Union filed its answer on August 2, 2024. Shaffer and Brian jointly filed their answer on 
September 8, 2024. 
{¶5} On December 12, 2024, U.S. Bank National filed a motion for default 
judgment against Ca pital One National Association, The Huntington National Bank, 
successor by merger to Sky Bank, and John Doe, Name Unknown, Unknown Spouse, if 
any of Theresa A. Shaffer. The same day, U.S. Bank National filed a motion for summary 
judgment on the claims against Shaffer and Brian. Shaffer and Brian jointly filed a 
response in opposition to U.S. Bank National’s motion for summary judgment on February 
13, 2025. 

1. The Unknown Spouse of Brian Shaffer, as designated in the complaint, was dismissed from the action 
on December 3, 2024. 

PAGE 3 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
{¶6} On March 18, 2025, Shaffer and Brian also filed a joint motion for summary 
judgment wherein they argued that the complaint was barred by the statute of limitations 
and that U.S. Bank National lacked standing. 
{¶7} On May 19, 2025, Shaffer filed a motion for leave to file a counterclaim. U.S. 
Bank National opposed the motion. 
{¶8} On August 7, 2025, the trial court denied Shaffer’s motion to amend her 
answer to include additional counterclaims. The trial court also granted in part and denied 
in part, U.S. Bank National’s motion for summary judgment and denied Shaffer and 
Brian’s joint motion for summary judgment in its entirety. The trial court concluded: 
[T]here is some disagreement among courts as to whether 
expiration of the six -year statute of limitations found in R.C. 
1303.16(A) applies to preclude foreclosure under a note. 
However, this Court believes the more reasonable approach 
is to honor the twenty -one-year statute of limitations for 
foreclosure on mortgages as contained in R.C. 2305.04. . . . 

Consequently, the Bank's [motion for summary judgment] is 
DENIED for being time -barred relative to claims for amounts 
owed under the Note. However, the Bank's [motion for 
summary judgment] is GRANTED with respect to its claim for 
foreclosure under the Mortgage. 

{¶9} Additionally, the trial court granted U.S. Bank National’s motion for default 
as to the parties that failed to timely answer or otherwise respond to the complaint. On 
August 8, 2025, Shaffer filed a motion for reconsideration.2 
{¶10} On August 11, 2025, the trial court filed its Judgment Entry and Foreclosure 
Decree. The trial court found, 
[O]n the evidence adduced that there is due to [U.S. Bank 
National] on the promissory note set forth in the First Count of 
the Complaint (the "Note"), the sum of $142,118.85 plus 
interest at 6.6500% per annum from March 1, 2018, for which 

2. The trial court denied the motion on August 25, 2025. 

PAGE 4 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
sum judgment is rendered, in rem, in favor of [U.S.] Bank 
National. 

. . . 

The Court further finds that the conditions in the Mortgage 
have been broken and the same has become absolute and 
[U.S. Bank National] is entitled to have the equity of 
redemption and dower of all Defendants in and to the 
Premises foreclosed. 

{¶11} The trial court’s entry further determined: 
While finding that there is no just reason for delay as to the 
Plaintiff's claim, the Judge makes no finding at this time as to 
the claims, rights, titles, interests or liens of the Defendants 
LCE Federal Credit Union and John Carroll University as set 
forth in their pleadings filed herein, except to note that such 
claims, rights, titles, interests or liens of the hereinabove 
Defendants are hereby ordered transferred to the proceeds 
derived from the sale of said premises, after the payment of 
the costs of the within action, taxes due and payable and the 
amount hereinabove found due Plaintiff, and the same is 
hereby ordered continued until further order. 

The Court further finds that there is no just reason for delay in 
entering the judgment herein. 

{¶12} On September 9, 2025, Shaffer filed a pro se motion for relief from judgment 
requesting that the trial court grant her motion for summary judgment and her motion for 
for leave to file a counterclaim, and to dismiss the complaint.3 Additionally, Shaffer filed a 
pro se motion to stay proceedings and to waive bond.4 
{¶13} The following day, on September 10, 2025, Shaffer filed her notice of 
appeal. 

3. On September 11, 2025, the trial court denied Shaffer’s motion for relief for lack of jurisdiction. 
4. The trial court denied Shaffer’s motion to stay and to waive bond on September 23, 2026. The trial court 
noted that it would reconsider the stay of judgment pending the posting of a supersedeas bond. 

PAGE 5 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
{¶14} On November 6, 2025, Shaffer, through counsel, filed a notice to stay 
proceedings as Shaffer had filed a petition in voluntary bankruptcy. U.S. Bank National 
filed a motion to withdraw the property from the scheduled sheriff’s sale the same day. 
The trial court granted the motion to withdraw the sale and ordered all proceedings stayed 
pending the disposition of the petition in bankruptcy. 
{¶15} On February 13, 2026, Shaffer filed a combined motion to stay sheriff's sale 
and to waive supersedeas bond. The trial court ordered that the sheriff's sale of the 
subject property be stayed pending final resolution of Shaffer's appeal upon the posting 
of a supersedeas bond in the amount of $25,000. 
The Appeal 
{¶16} Shaffer raises three assignments of error for review: 
[1.] The trial court erred in granting [ U.S. Bank National]’s 
motion for summary judgment. 

[2.] The trial court erred in denying [Shaffer]’s motion for 
summary judgment. 

[3.] The trial court erred in denying [Shaffer]’s motion for leave 
to file her counterclaims. 

{¶17} As a preliminary matter, before addressing Shaffer’s assignments of error, 
we must first determine whether the trial court’s entry is a final appealable order. 
{¶18} According to Ohio Const., art. IV, § 3(B)(2), a judgment of a trial court can 
be immediately reviewed by an appellate court only if it constitutes a “final order” in the 
action. Bank of Am. v. Telerico, 2017-Ohio-1339, ¶ 3 (11th Dist.), citing In re Biddlestone, 
2011-Ohio-1299, ¶ 3 (11th Dist.). A reviewing court has no jurisdiction to review the matter 
if the lower court’s order is not final, and the matter must be dismissed. Id., citing Gen. 
Acc. Ins. Co. v. Ins. Co. of N. Am ., 44 Ohio St.3d 17, 20 (1989). “For a judgment to be 

PAGE 6 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
final and appealable, it must satisfy the requirements of R.C. 2505.02 and, if applicable, 
Civ.R. 54(B).” Id. 
{¶19} R.C. 2505.02(B) defines a final order as one of the following: 
(1) An order that affects a substantial right in an action that 
in effect determines the action and prevents a judgment 

(2) An order that affects a substantial right made in a 
special proceeding or upon a summary application in an 
action after judgment; 

(3) An order that vacates or sets aside a judgment or 
grants a new trial; 

(4) An order that grants or denies a provisional remedy 
and to which both of the following apply: 

(a) The order in effect determines the action with 
respect to the provisional remedy and prevents a 
judgment in the action in favor of the appealing party 
with respect to the provisional remedy. 

(b) The appealing party would not be afforded a 
meaningful or effective remedy by an appeal following 
final judgment as to all proceedings, issues, claims, 
and parties in the action. 

(5) An order that determines that an action may or may not 
be maintained as a class action; 

(6) An order determining the constitutionality of any 
changes to the Revised Code . . . ; 

(7) An order in an appropriation proceeding . . . .” 

{¶20} There are two stages to foreclosure actions. Each stage results in a final, 
appealable judgment: the foreclosure decree and the confirmation of sale. See Farmers 
State Bank v. Sponaugle , 2019-Ohio-2518, ¶ 18. “The order of foreclosure determines 
the extent of each lienholder's interest, sets out the priority of the liens, determines the 
other rights and responsibilities of each party, and orders the property to be sold by 

PAGE 7 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
sheriff's sale.” Id. at ¶ 18, citing CitiMortgage, Inc. v. Roznowski, 2014-Ohio-1984, ¶ 39, 
and R.C. 2323.07. 
{¶21} An order that fails to reflect the necessary components of a foreclosure 
judgment—such as determining the extent of each lienholder's interest —is not a final 
appealable order. Bank of New York Mellon v. Cox , 2025-Ohio-4406, ¶ 12 (12th Dist.), 
citing Johnson v. Stone, 2019-Ohio-4630, ¶ 19 (3d Dist.) (concluding that order was not 
a final order because the trial court did not determine the extent of each lienholder's 
interest); see also Gemmell v. Evergreen Site Holdings, Inc., 2025-Ohio-2258, ¶ 18 (4th 
Dist.). 
{¶22} In the trial court’s August 11, 2025 entry, the court stated: 
The Judge further finds that Defendants LCE Federal Credit 
Union and John Carroll University each claims some rights, 
titles, interests, claims, or liens upon the Premises, as set forth 
in the pleading they filed herein but that any rights, titles, 
interests, claims, or liens that they may have are inferior and 
subsequent to the lien of Plaintiff. . . 

the Judge makes no finding at this time as to the claims, 
rights, titles, interests or liens of the Defendants LCE Federal 
Credit Union and John Carroll University as set forth in their 
pleadings filed herein, except to note that such claims, rights, 
titles, interes ts or liens of the hereinabove Defendants are 
hereby ordered transferred to the proceeds derived from the 
sale of said premises. . . 

{¶23} We conclude that the trial court’s August 11, 2025 entry is not a final 
appealable order as it does not determine or establish the priority of two of the junior 
lienholders. Tax Ease Ohio L .L.C. v. Miller , 2019 -Ohio-3433, ¶ 10 (5th

leads.caseName: Whidbey Enviromental Action Network, V. City Of Oak Harbor
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF WASHINGTON 
DIVISION ONE 

WHIDBEY ENVIRONMENTAL 
ACTION NETWORK, 

 Appellant, 

 v. 

CITY OF OAK HARBOR, 

 Respondent. 
No. 88228-7-I 

 UNPUBLISHED OPINION 

BOWMAN, A.C.J. — Sound Development Group LLC proposed a hotel 
project to the city of Oak Harbor that would use portions of Hal Ramaley 
Memorial Park for a parking lot. To facilitate transfer of the park property, the 
City passed Oak Harbor Ordinance 1999 to amend former Oak Harbor Municipal 
Code (OHMC) 1.30.010 (2014), removing the requirement that the public 
approve the sale of park property by vote. The amendment authorized the sale 
of park property without a public vote if, after review of a development agreement 
between the City and a private entity, the sale would be beneficial to the City 
using predefined criteria. Whidbey Environmental Action Network (WEAN) sued 
the City, alleging, among other things, that the City violated Washington’s State 
Environmental Policy Act (SEPA), chapter 43.21C RCW, by passing the 
ordinance before reviewing any adverse environmental impacts it may have. The 
City moved for summary judgment, arguing that the ordinance did not trigger 

No. 88228-7-I/2 
2 
SEPA review. The trial court granted summary judgment for the City, and WEAN 
appeals. We reverse the trial court’s order on summary judgment and remand 
for further proceedings. 
FACTS 
On September 6, 2023, Sound Development submitted to the City a 
proposal for a commercial and residential project on land parcels next to Hal 
Ramaley Memorial Park. The proposal included a one-story brewpub building 
with single-story residential units and a parking lot behind the pub. The City 
rejected the proposal and encouraged Sound Development to propose a building 
project with “more urban density, pedestrian activity, and business activity for 
downtown.” 
Sound Development then proposed “Home2 Suites by Hilton Hotels,” a 
four-story hotel with 107 rooms and convention meeting spaces. The proposal 
included a parking lot that would encroach on portions of the park. As a result, 
Raymond Lindenburg, a senior planner in the City’s Department of Development 
Services, “worked with Sound Development to outline a potential swap or sale of 
park land.” During that process, Lindenburg collaborated with the City attorney, 
who determined that former OHMC 1.30.010 required the City to obtain citizen 
approval in an election before disposing of developed park property.1 
On March 11, 2024, Lindenburg informed developer Sean Byrne about the 
code requirement and presented potential “path[s] forward . . . for the land swap 

1 See Oak Harbor Ordinance 1728 (requiring citizen approval in an election 
before disposing of developed City park property unless the property “is required to 
accomplish a necessary public purpose”). 
No. 88228-7-I/3 
3 
and additional parking for the site.” Option (1) was to hold a vote under the 
current ordinance, former OHMC 1.30.010. Option (2) was to remove the fourth 
floor of the hotel to reduce the need for additional parking. Option (3) was to 
eliminate the pool and other amenities to make space for more parking. And 
option (4) was to amend former OHMC 1.30.010. Byrne addressed the fourth 
option, telling Lindenburg they should “identify the scope and timeline” of a code 
amendment. On March 28, Lindenburg told Byrne that “[s]taff is working on a 
draft ordinance to revise the code to not require a municipal election to dispose 
of/sell city park properties.” While the City drafted an amendment to former 
OHMC 1.30.010, Sound Development moved forward with their plans for the 
hotel project. 
On August 13, 2024, the City council held a public hearing on Ordinance 
1999, which would amend former OHMC 1.30.010 to “remove the requirement 
for voter approval prior to sale or trade of developed park property under specific 
circumstances.” Lindenburg presented the ordinance at the hearing, explaining 
its purpose was “to streamline the process of potentially transferring land that is 
designated as park property.” He said that “[t]he proposed language revision 
was spurred by a proposal for a new hotel project located adjacent to Hal 
Ramaley Park” and recommended approval of the ordinance. Several residents 
spoke in opposition of Ordinance 1999. At the end of the meeting, the council 
members passed Ordinance 1999 with a six-to-one vote. 
No. 88228-7-I/4 
4 
Ordinance 1999 amended former OHMC 1.30.010 by providing two more 
circumstances for when the City council could dispose of developed City park 
property without citizen approval.2 Ordinance 1999 provides, in relevant part: 
(2) Developed city park property shall not be disposed of in any 
manner without citizen approval in an election, except when 
presented, reviewed, and approved at a public hearing that meets 
at least one of the following criteria: 

(a) The city council reviews a development agreement 
between the city and private entity and determines that; the 
property exchange is calculated at a one-to-one ratio of land 
area or greater in benefit to the city, the privately owned land 
offered in exchange is of equal or greater market value than 
the publicly owned land, and the private land offered is an 
appropriate replacement for the public property to be 
granted. The city council shall determine that the property 
exchange is beneficial to the city based on park needs, 
location, environmental standards and accessibility to park 
users and in its discretion approve a development 
agreement. 

(b) The city council reviews a development agreement 
between the city and private entity and determines that the 
value of physical infrastructure to city park land or 
improvements to city park land provided by the private entity 
is at least 150 [percent] of the market value of the land 
granted by the city to the private entity. Such values shall be 
determined by all parties in a mutually agreed development 
agreement approved by the city council. 

On August 15, 2024, Lindenburg informed Byrne that Ordinance 1999 
passed, stating: 
As you may have heard, Ordinance 1999 amending the election 
requirement for transfer of park land was approved on Tuesday. 
I’ve attached the revised code as adopted, let me know if there are 
any questions you have. I think that the last time we talked, we 
discussed the idea of including the walkway between [SE] Pioneer 
[Way] and [SE] Bayshore [Drive] as a part of a land swap that could 

2 Compare Ordinance 1728, with Ordinance 1999. 
No. 88228-7-I/5 
5 
be counted, to make up for the dedication of the land along Pioneer 
Way, which could not be counted toward the total. 

As always, let me know if you need any assistance or want to talk 
about future planning and process. 

On August 30, 2024, WEAN sued the City, seeking a declaratory 
judgment that the passage of Ordinance 1999 violated SEPA because the City 
failed to first evaluate the potential environmental impacts of the ordinance.3 On 
January 27, 2025, the City moved for summary judgment, asking the trial court to 
dismiss WEAN’s lawsuit. It argued that Ordinance 1999 was not subject to 
SEPA review because it is not an “action” under the statutory scheme and, in any 
event, is categorically exempt from review under WAC 197-11-800(19). 
On May 1, 2025, after a hearing, the court entered a written order 
concluding, among other things, that Ordinance 1999 “was not a covered action 
subject to SEPA review” and was “categorically exempt from SEPA review” 
under WAC 197-11-800(19)(a) and (b). The court granted the City’s motion for 
summary judgment and dismissed WEAN’s lawsuit with prejudice. 
WEAN appeals. 
ANALYSIS 
WEAN argues the trial court erred by granting summary judgment 
because the City violated SEPA when it passed Ordinance 1999 without first 
evaluating the ordinance’s potential environmental impacts. It contends 

3 WEAN also sought a writ of certiorari, alleging that the adoption of the 
ordinance was arbitrary and capricious under article IV, section 6 of the Washington 
Constitution and that passing Ordinance 1999 violated Washington’s code of ethics for 
municipal officers under RCW 42.23.070(1). Those allegations are not at issue on 
appeal. 
No. 88228-7-I/6 
6 
Ordinance 1999 is a “nonproject action” that is not categorially exempt from 
SEPA review. We address both arguments in turn. 
We review a trial court’s summary judgment order de novo, viewing the 
facts in a light most favorable to the nonmoving party. Columbia Riverkeeper v. 
Port of Vancouver USA, 188 Wn.2d 80, 90, 392 P.3d 1025 (2017). Summary 
judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine issue of material fact and the 
moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Id.; CR 56(c). We apply 
the rules of statutory construction to local ordinances. Morawek v. City of 
Bonney Lake, 184 Wn. App. 487, 492, 337 P.3d 1097 (2014). “When an 
ordinance is unambiguous, construction is not necessary, because the plain 
meaning controls.” Id. 
“SEPA acts as a full disclosure directive to consider any potential 
environmental impacts of a project.” King County v. Friends of Sammamish 
Valley, 3 Wn.3d 793, 815, 556 P.3d 132 (2024). The purposes of SEPA are to 
(1) encourage productive and enjoyable harmony between humankind and the 
environment, (2) promote efforts that will prevent or eliminate damage to the 
environment or biosphere, (3) stimulate the health and welfare of human beings, 
and (4) enrich the understanding of ecological systems and natural resources. 
RCW 43.21C.010. SEPA attempts to shape the state’s environment by 
deliberation, not default. Stempel v. Dep’t of Water Res., 82 Wn.2d 109, 118, 
508 P.2d 166 (1973). 

No. 88228-7-I/7 
7 
1. Nonproject Action under SEPA 
WEAN argues that Ordinance 1999 qualifies as a nonproject action 
subject to SEPA review under WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(i).4 We agree. 
Generally, SEPA requires that a “government conduct environmental 
review, through at least a threshold determination, for any proposal that meets 
the definition of an action.” Pub. Utility Dist. No. 1 of Clark County v. Pollution 
Control Hr’gs Bd., 137 Wn. App. 150, 158, 151 P.3d 1067 (2007). “Under SEPA, 
the definition of ‘action’ covers just about everything.” Friends of Sammamish 
Valley, 3 Wn.3d at 815. Actions under SEPA include, among other things, “[n]ew 
or revised agency rules, regulations, plans, policies, or procedures” and 
“[l]egislative proposals.” WAC 197-11-704(1)(b), (c). And they fall within one of 
two categories—project actions and nonproject actions. Friends of Sammamish 
Valley, 3 Wn.3d at 815; WAC 197-11-704(2)(a), (b). 
A “project action” “involves a decision on a specific project, such as a 
construction or management activity located in a defined geographic area.” WAC 
197-11-704(2)(a). “Nonproject actions” are “broader than a single site specific 
project.” WAC 197-11-774. They “involve decisions on policies, plans, or 
programs,” including the “adoption or amendment of legislation, ordinances, 
rules, or regulations that contain standards controlling use or modification of the 
environment.” WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(i). 

4 After oral argument, we asked the parties to submit supplemental briefing on 
whether WAC 197-11-704(2)(b)(iii) applies to Ordinance 1999. After reviewing the 
briefs, we conclude that it does not.

benefit to the city” or that (2) the value of physical infrastructure to City park land 
or improvements to the City park by the private entity is “at least 150 [percent] of

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
 FOR THE DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA

____________________________________
 )
ERIC MUSSHORN, )
 )
 Plaintiff, )
 )
 v. ) Civil Action No. 24-3507 (PLF)
 )
HUNG CAO, 1 )
Secretary of the Navy, )
 )
 Defendant. )
____________________________________)

 OPINION

 Eric Musshorn (“LT Musshorn”), an active duty Naval Service Lieutenant, brings

this action against the Secretary of the Navy (“the Secretary”) under the Administrative

Procedure Act (“APA”), 5 U.S.C. § 701 et. seq., seeking review of a final agency decision by the

Board for Correction of Naval Records (“BCNR” or “the Board”). See Complaint (“Compl.”)

[Dkt. No. 1] at 1. This matter is before the Court on the parties’ cross-motions for summary

judgment. See Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Plfs. Mot.”) [Dkt. No. 11];

Defendant’s Cross Motion for Summary Judgment (“Defs. Mot.”) [Dkt. No. 14]. The Court

granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment and denied LT Musshorn’s cross-motion on

September 30, 2026. This Opinion explains the reasoning underlying that Order. 2

 1
 Pursuant to Rule 25(d)(1) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Hung Cao, the
current Acting Secretary of the Navy, has been substituted for former Secretary of the Navy
Carlos Del Toro as the named defendant in this case.
 2
 The papers reviewed by the Court in connection with this matter include:
Complaint (“Compl.”) [Dkt. No. 1]; Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment and
  I. BACKGROUND

 A. Statutory Background

 Section 533 of Title 10 of the United States Code governs the determination of the

grade and rank “of a person receiving an original appointment in a commissioned grade” in the

United States Navy. 10 U.S.C. § 533(a)(1). Such person “shall be credited at the time of such

appointment with any active commissioned service . . . that he performed in any armed force . . .

before such appointment.” Id. Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 533 “[t]he Secretary of Defense shall

prescribe regulations, which shall apply uniformly among the Army, Navy, Air Force, and

Marine Corps, to authorize the Secretary of the military department concerned to limit the

amount of prior active commissioned service with which a person receiving an original

appointment may be credited under paragraph (1), or to deny any such credit, in the case of a

person who at the time of such appointment is credited with constructive service under

subsection (b).” Id. § 533(a)(2).

 Pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 533(a)(2), the Secretary of Defense promulgated

Department of Defense Directive 1312.03 (“DoDI 1312.03”), dated December 28, 2018. See

DoDI 1312.03 at AR0082-92. DoDI 1312.03 provides:

 Subject to the limitations in this section, a person’s entry grade,
 date of rank, and service in grade for promotion eligibility will be
 determined by the amount of entry grade credit awarded upon
 original appointment. The amount of entry grade credit will equal

Memorandum of Law in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Plfs. Mot.”)
[Dkt. No. 11]; Defendant’s Cross Motion and Memorandum of Points and Authorities in
Opposition to Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment, and in Support of Defendant’s Cross-
Motion for Summary Judgment (“Defs. Mot.”) [Dkt. No. 14]; Plaintiff’s Opposition to
Defendant’s Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment and Reply to Defendant’s Opposition to
Plaintiff’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Plfs. Reply”) [Dkt. No. 16]; Defendant’s
Memorandum in Further Support of Cross-Motion for Summary Judgment (“Defs. Reply”) [Dkt.
No. 20]; and the Joint Appendix (“App.”) [Dkt. No. 21].

 2
  the sum of the prior commissioned service credit and the
 constructive service credit a person is given.

DoDI 1312.03 ¶ 3.1. For appointments for regular (as opposed to reserve) officers, credit for

prior commissioned service “will be awarded on a day-for-day basis for any active

commissioned service.” Id. ¶ 3.2.a. DoDI 1312.03 permits two exceptions to this general rule.

First, pursuant to Paragraph 3.2.c:

 The Secretaries of the Military Departments may limit the amount
 of credit for prior commissioned service in a field other than the
 professional specialty for which the person is currently being
 appointed, but will award no less than a half day credit for each
 day of such service.

Id. ¶ 3.2.c. Second, pursuant to Paragraph 3.2.d:

 The Secretary of the Military Department concerned may deny
 prior commissioned service credit for each day of constructive
 service credit a person who is not currently a regular officer or a
 reserve officer in an active status receives for the education,
 training, or experience required for appointment, designation, or
 assignment as a judge advocate in a Military Department, as a
 chaplain, or in other officer career fields as designated by the
 Secretaries of the Military Departments.

Id. ¶ 3.2.d.

 Chief of Naval Operations Instruction 1120.11A (“OPNAVINST 1120.11A”),

dated July 14, 2015, established Navy-specific regulations governing the award of entry grade

credit (“EGC”) under 10 U.S.C. § 533 and 10 U.S.C. § 12207, providing guidance for the

“[a]ppointment of officers in the Judge Advocate Generals Corps (JAGC).” See

OPNAVINST 1120.11A ¶¶ 1.a(1), 1.a(3) at AR0116. OPNAVINST 1120.11A provided that

“total entry grade credit granted, other than for officers accessed through [the Navy’s Law

Education Program (“LEP”)], will be limited to 48 months” in order to “obtain experienced

former active duty commissioned officers . . . while maintaining uniform and stable management

 3
 of the JAGC community.” Id. ¶ 11 at AR0123. This limitation could be waived for various

reasons, including “when a gross inequity to the applicant would otherwise result.” Id.

¶¶ 11.a(1)-(3) at AR0124. OPNAVINST 1120.11A was superseded by DoDI 1312.03. See

Defs. Mot. at 8.

 A memorandum from the Chief of Naval Personnel (“CNP Memo”), dated

April 11, 2023, provides additional guidance for the computation of EGC for JAGC appointees

in accordance with DoDI 1312.03. See CNP Memo at AR0024-25. The CNP Memo states that

EGC will be calculated as the sum of an officer’s total prior commissioned service credit

(“PCSC”) and total constructive service credit (“CSC”). See CNP Memo ¶ 1.b at AR0024.

More specifically, for officers with PCSC in a field other than JAGC,

 such [PCSC] will be calculated at a half day for each day of total
 prior active commissioned service. The amount of CSC awarded
 will then be deducted from the calculated amount of [PCSC]. The
 sum will be the total amount of [PCSC] awarded, which will then
 be added to the CSC awarded, resulting in the total EGC awarded.

Id. ¶ 1.c. For example, a JAGC applicant “with 10 years of [PCSC] as a submarine officer will

be awarded as such: EGC = [PCSC] + CSC. [PCSC] = 10 years X 50% = 5 years - 3 years CSC

= 2 years [PCSC] total. CSC = 3 years. EGC = 2 years ([PCSC] total) + 3 years (CSC) = 5

years.” Id.

 B. Factual Background

 LT Musshorn enlisted in the United States Air Force, Texas Air National Guard,

on April 16, 2003. (The Complaint lists his enlistment date as May 7, 2003.). See Plfs. Mot. at 9;

 4
 Compl. ¶ 24. 3 He later served as an active-duty officer in the Air Force from his commission in

April 2007 until his transition to the Connecticut Air National Guard in February 2016. Plfs.

Mot. at 9. LT Musshorn then served on active duty orders for 437 days, from April 1, 2016 to

July 20, 2017, including a combat deployment to Iraq and Syria. Id. He was promoted to the

rank of O-4 on December 3, 2016. Id.

 While serving in the Connecticut Air National Guard, LT Musshorn attended the

University of Maine School of Law from Fall 2017 to Spring 2020. Plfs. Mot. at 9. In

February 2020, he passed the Uniform Bar Exam in Vermont and was subsequently admitted to

practice in Vermont and Texas. Id. at 9-10. LT Musshorn then applied for and was offered

appointment to the Navy’s JAGC. Id. at 10. He was initially assured that he would “receive one

half day credit for each day of his prior active commissioned service plus 3 years of constructive

service credit for law school totaling approximately 8 years of EGC,” allowing him to either

maintain his 0-4 rank upon commissioning with the JAGC or qualify for 0-4 at the conclusion of

his initial 2-year commitment. See id. at 10. On May 12, 2020, LT Musshorn signed a

conditional release for interservice transfer to the Navy, which was approved on June 17, 2020.

Plfs. Mot. at 10. On July 10, 2020, he requested ten years of EGC for his prior active

commissioned service to maintain his current military grade of O-4. Id. While his request was

pending, LT Musshorn transferred from the Air National Guard to the Navy on August 9, 2021.

Id.

 On August 10, 2021, LT Musshorn was appointed to the JAGC as an O-3

Lieutenant with 4 years of EGC, with an effective date of rank of August 1, 2021. See Plfs. Mot.

 3
 Citations to LT Musshorn’s Motion for Summary Judgment (“Plfs. Mot.”) and
Reply to Defendant’s Opposition (“Plfs. Reply”) are to the ECF-generated pagination.

 5
 at 10. On November 21, 2022, the Chief of Naval Personnel (“CNP”) denied LT Musshorn’s

request for 10 years EGC, citing OPNAVINST 1120.11A and directed him to petition the Board

for additional relief. See id. (citing Letter from CNP at AR0166). LT Musshorn petitioned the

BCNR in February 2023 and requested an award of additional EGC for his prior active

commissioned service in accordance with Department of Defense Instruction 1312.03. Id. at 10-

11 (citing Application for Correction of Military Record at AR0067-68). His case was assigned

docket number NR202300001094. See id. at 11.

 On March 9, 2023, the Bureau of Naval Personnel’s Office of Legal Counsel

provided an advisory opinion to the Board (“First Advisory Opinion”). See First Advisory

Opinion at AR0047-50; Plfs. Mot. at 11; Defs. Mot. at 3. The First Advisory Opinion explained

that because “DoD Instruction 1312.02 supersedes OPNAVIST 1120.11A for EGC calculation,”

its 48-month limitation of EGC was inapplicable. See First Advisory Opinion at AR0049-50.

The First Advisory Opinion concluded that LT Musshorn’s petition “should be approved in

part,” and the Board should refer the matter to the CNP for recalculation of LT Musshorn’s EGC

in accordance with DoDI 1312.03, subject to his discretion. See id. at AR0050. LT Musshorn

submitted a response to the First Advisory Opinion, requesting that the BCNR “consider the

policy identified in DoDI 1312.03 combined with the ability to waive the 48-month cap in

OPNAVINST 1120.11A when a ‘gross inequity’ would occur” and “correct his records to reflect

10 years of EGC.” See Plfs. Mot. at 11 (citing AR0059-65).

 On September 26, 2023, the Office of Legal Counsel prepared a second advisory

opinion (“Second Advisory Opinion”). See Second Advisory Opinion at AR0021-23. The

Second Advisory Opinion agreed that LT Musshorn’s EGC was erroneously calculated under

OPNAVIST 1120.11A, “which limited EGC to applicants such as Petitioner to 48 months.” Id.

 6
 at AR0021. “Applying the standards of DoD Instruction 1312.03,” as “currently [calculated] in

accordance with the [CNP Memo],” it concluded that LT Musshorn was entitled to 4.8 years

(1,752 days) of EGC. Id. at AR0022. This calculation applied “both permissive reductions set

forth in the Department of Defense regulations.” See Defs. Mot. at 3. The Second Advisory

Opinion also outlined three alternative options: “(1) The Board could determine that in the

absence of [the CNP memo], that Petitioner is entitled to full EGC, without the two Secretarial

authority limitations permitted by DoD Instruction 1312.03,” resulting in an EGC of

approximately 12.7 years; (2) the Board could “apply the Secretary’s authority to limit prior

commissioned service for service in a different professional specialty . . . but not apply the

second Secretarial authority to suppress prior

Ohio-4091.] 

NOTICE 
This slip opinion is subject to formal revision before it is published in an 
advance sheet of the Ohio Official Reports. Readers are requested to 
promptly notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of Ohio, 65 
South Front Street, Columbus, Ohio 43215, of any typographical or other 
formal errors in the opinion, in order that corrections may be made before 
the opinion is published. 

SLIP OPINION NO. 2026-OHIO-4091 
THE STATE EX REL. SOMMERS DEVELOPMENT GROUP, L.L.C. v. CUYAHOGA 
COUNTY BOARD OF ELECTIONS . 
[Until this opinion appears in the Ohio Official Reports advance sheets, it 
may be cited as State ex rel. Sommers Dev. Group, L.L.C. v. Cuyahoga Cty. Bd. 
of Elections, Slip Opinion No. 2026-Ohio-4091.] 
Elections—Prohibition—Mandamus—Writs sought to remove an initiative 
ordinance from November 2026 general -election ballot —Relator’s claim 
not barred by doctrine of laches, because it did not unreasonably delay in 
asserting a right—Relator failed to show that board of elections abused its 
discretion or clearly disregarded applicable law in placing initiative 
ordinance on ballot and denying relator’s protest—Writs denied. 
(No. 2026-1307—Submitted October 13, 2026—Decided October 19, 2026.) 
IN PROHIBITION and MANDAMUS. 
__________________ 
The per curiam opinion below was joined by KENNEDY, C.J., and FISCHER, 
DEWINE, BRUNNER, DETERS, HAWKINS, and SHANAHAN, JJ. 
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 

2 

Per Curiam. 
{¶ 1} In this expedited election case, relator, Sommers Development Group, 
L.L.C. (“Sommers”), seeks a writ of prohibition or a writ of mandamus ordering 
respondent, the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections , to remove an initiative 
ordinance from the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot. Sommers plans to 
build a townhome community on real property located in the City of Mayfield 
Heights. In May 2026, the Mayfield Heights City Council rezoned the property 
from “Headquarters or Executive Offices Park District s” to “Planned Unit 
Development District s, Minimum Three Acr es.” A citizen’s committee (“ the 
petition committee”) submitted a signed initiative petition to the city council to 
return the zoning to “Headquarters or Executive Offices Park Districts,” which the 
city council certified to the board of elections for placement on the ballot. Sommers 
filed a protest against the petition with the board , which the board denied after 
conducting a hearing. 
{¶ 2} Sommers argues that the initiative ordinance should be removed from 
the ballot for four reasons: (1) the initiative petition was disguised as an untimely 
referendum petition, (2) the initiative ordinance constitutes an administrative 
action, (3) the petition committee and the city council did not comply with the 
requirements of the Mayfield Heights Charter for placing an initiative ordinance on 
the ballot, and (4) the city council certified the initiative petition to the board of 
elections after the statutory-certification deadline. 
{¶ 3} For the following reasons, we deny the writs. 
I. BACKGROUND 
A. Legal Background 
{¶ 4} Mayfield Heights is a chartered municipality. Under Article II, 
Section 1f of the Ohio Constitution, “[t]he initiative and referendum powers are . . . 
reserved to the people of each municipality on all questions which such 
January Term, 2026 

3 
municipalities may . . . be authorized by law to control by legislative action; such 
powers shall be exercised in the manner . . . provided by law.” 
{¶ 5} The city charter provides for the exercise of initiative and referendum 
rights. Article VIII, Section 1 of the city charter provides for the right of initiative, 
stating that “[t]he electors of the City shall have power to propose any ordinance or 
resolution, except an ordinance for the appropriation of money, and to adopt or 
reject the same at the polls.” Article VIII, Section 2 of the city charter provides for 
the right to referendum, stating that “[t]he electors of the City shall have the power 
to approve or reject at the polls any ordinance or resolution passed by the Council 
except as hereinafter provided.” 
B. Factual Background 
{¶ 6} Sommers is a party to a contract with Rockwell Automation, Inc., 
which it negotiated for the purpose of redeveloping real property located in 
Mayfield Heights into a townhome community. Sommers is the property 
developer; Rockwell Automation owns the property. 
{¶ 7} At one time , the property was zoned under the U -7 classification, 
which applies to “Headquarters or Executive Offices Park District s.” But to 
implement its plan to redevelop the property, Sommers requested that the city 
council rezone the property from the U -7 classification to the U -2A(1) 
classification, the latter of which applies to “Planned Unit Development District s, 
Minimum Three Acres.” Sommers also requested approval of a preliminary site 
plan and requested a variance from the U -2A(1) classification to allow for 
additional site development. 
{¶ 8} On May 27, 2026, the city council held a meeting at which it adopted 
an ordinance granting a zoning amendment that rezoned the property to the U -
2A(1) classification. At the same meeting, the city council adopted a resolution 
approving the Mayfield Heights B oard of Zoning Appeals’ grant of a density 
variance to the property. 
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 

4 
{¶ 9} On July 24, a committee opposed to the project filed an initiative 
petition with the city council, seeking an ordinance that would return the zoning of 
the property to the U-7 classification. In an affidavit, Brian Wright, the person who 
submitted the petition, attests that he went to the Mayfield Heights City Hall during 
its posted business hours to deliver the petition to the clerk of council. Wright was 
required to use an intercom to enter the city hall, but no one responded when he 
used the intercom, so he went to the office of the Mayfield Heights P olice 
Department, which is part of the city -hall compound. He explained to the police 
officer at the counter that he had a document to deliver to the clerk of council. A 
few moments later, a woman who identified herself as the mayor’s assistant arrived. 
She said that the clerk of council was out of town but that she could accept the 
document. Wright gave her the initiative petition, but when she signed a form 
indicating receipt of the petition, she crossed out the words “Clerk of Council.” 
The receipt form as signed by the assistant provides that on July 24, 17 part -
petitions containing approximately 535 signatures were delivered to the “ Clerk of 
Council.” 
{¶ 10} On August 18, the city council held a hearing on the initiative 
petition, but it did not vote on the petition. 
{¶ 11} On September 1, the city council held a special meeting, at which it 
voted four to three to reject the initiative petition. 
{¶ 12} On September 2, the petition committee filed a supplemental 
initiative petition, ostensibly for the purpose of obtaining additional signatures. 
Two days later, the board of elections advised the clerk of council that the initiative 
petition—inclusive of the original and supplemental part-petitions—had 691 valid 
signatures, which no one disputes was sufficient to meet the minimum number 
required by law. 
{¶ 13} On September 9, the city council adopted an emergency resolution 
authorizing the clerk of council to certify the initiative petition to the board of 
January Term, 2026 

5 
elections for placement on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot. The next 
day, Sommers filed a protest with the board, outlining its objections to the petition. 
{¶ 14} On September 21, the board of elections held a protest hearing, 
which included the presentation by Sommers of documentary evidence and 
argument supporting its request that the board grant its protest. At the conclusion 
of the hearing, the board denied the protest. 
{¶ 15} Sommers filed this original action four days later. Sommers requests 
a writ of prohibition preventing the board of elections from certifying and placing 
the initiative ordinance on the November 3, 2026 general -election ballot, adding 
that if ballots have already been prepared, the board should be barred from counting 
or certifying votes cast on the ordinance. Alternatively, Sommers requests a writ 
of mandamus ordering the board to grant its protest and remove the initiative 
ordinance from the ballot, adding that if ballots have already been prepared, the 
votes cast on the ordinance should not be counted or certified. The members of the 
petition committee, Robert K. Agresta, Diane M. Agresta, Iwona Tietz -Golczak, 
Marcin B. Golczak, and Elvera Ranallo, filed a motion to intervene as respondents, 
which we granted. 2026-Ohio-3896. 
II. LEGAL ANALYSIS 
A. Laches 
{¶ 16} The board of elections and the petition committee argue that we 
should deny the writs on the basis of laches. We disagree. 
{¶ 17} “‘“Extreme diligence and promptness are required in elections -
related matters.”’” State ex rel. Miller v. Union Cty. Bd. of Elections , 2023-Ohio-
3664, ¶ 18, quoting State ex rel. Clark v. Twinsburg, 2022-Ohio-3089, ¶ 11, quoting 
State ex rel. Commt. for the Charter Amendment, City Trash Collection v. Westlake, 
2002-Ohio-5302, ¶ 16. “‘Laches will bar an action when there is (1) an 
unreasonable delay or lapse of time in asserting a right, (2) the absence of an excuse 
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 

6 
for the delay, (3) actual or constructive knowledge of the injury or wrong, and 
(4) prejudice to the opposing party.’” Id., quoting Clark at ¶ 11. 
{¶ 18} On September 9, 2026, the city council adopted an emergency 
resolution authorizing the clerk of council to certify the initiative petition to the 
board of elections for placement on the November 3, 2026 general-election ballot. 
The next day, Sommers filed a protest with the board, outlining its objections to the 
petition. In addition, Sommers filed its complaint in this court four days after the 
board denied its protest. The board and the petition committee do not argue that 
either of these periods constitutes unreasonable delay. 
{¶ 19} Rather, the board of elections and the petition committee argue that 
Sommers should have act ed earlier, before the city council certified the initiative 
petition to the board, to prevent either the city council from considering the petition 
or the board from placing the initiative ordinance on the ballot. The board argues 
that Sommers could have filed an unspecified action in August to compel the city 
council to not consider the petition . The petition committee argues that Sommers 
could have filed a protest with the board earlier than it did. In support, the petition 
committee cites Mason City School Dist. v. Warren Cty. Bd. of Elections , 2005-
Ohio-5363. 
{¶ 20} In Mason, a petition was submitted to the Warren County Board of 
Elections under R.C. 5705.261 to place a school-district-levy decrease on the ballot. 
The petition was submitted to the board on May 24, 2005, but the board did not 
certify the petition to the ballot until August 16. The school district filed a protest 
against the petition with the board on August 22. We held that the school district 
“did not need to await the board of elections’ certification of the petition before [it] 
protested the petition.” Id. at ¶ 15. This holding implies that the school district 
could have filed its protest at any time after the petition was submitted to the board. 
See id. at ¶ 14, 16. We cited two other cases in which we held similarly. See id. at 
¶ 15, citing State ex rel. Ascani v. Stark Cty. Bd. of Elections, 1998-Ohio-586, ¶ 12 
January Term, 2026 

7 
(petition regarding a horse-racing satellite facility submitted under R.C. 3769.27) , 
and State ex

leads.caseName: Holy Trinity Ukrainian Catholic Church v. Township of Collier
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
leads.text:
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE THIRD CIRCUIT
 No. 26-2072

 HOLY TRINITY UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC CHURCH,
 Appellant

 v.

 TOWNSHIP OF COLLIER; GABE BENVENUTI; WAYNE
 CHIURAZZI; TIM DOWNEY, JR.; JULIE MURPHY; et al.
 _____________________________
 On Appeal from the U.S. District Court, W.D. Pa.
 Judge Christy Criswell Wiegand, No. 2:26-cv-00024

 Before: BIBAS, MATEY, and MONTGOMERY-REEVES,
 Circuit Judges
 Argued: Sept. 9, 2026; Filed: Oct. 19, 2026
 _____________________________

 OPINION OF THE COURT
 BIBAS, Circuit Judge. Preliminary injunctions exist to pre-
 serve cases, not decide them. Even when the merits are strong,
 courts may properly deny a preliminary injunction because the
 feared injury is reparable without preliminary relief, an injunc-
 tion would needlessly disrupt the status quo, or one is not
 needed to keep the case alive. All three are true here.
 A church says that its township violated federal law by
 denying its rezoning application. It seeks a preliminary injunc-
 tion and has a strong case on the merits; but it does not show
 why temporary relief is helpful, let alone necessary. So we will
AFFIRM the District Court’s denial of a preliminary injunction.

 I. THE ZONING BOARD BLOCKS A PRO-LIFE SHRINE
 Holy Trinity is a Ukrainian Catholic parish outside Pitts-
burgh. It practices the Catholic faith, but with rituals and archi-
tecture that are distinctively Ukrainian. The parish owns two
plots of land. On one of them, in Carnegie, sits a church, where
it holds regular liturgies. The other plot, in nearby Collier
Township, has been owned by the parish for more than seven
decades. That 41-acre plot houses the parish’s cemetery and
mausoleum but is otherwise mostly wooded.
 About three years ago, Holy Trinity’s pastor felt called to
turn the second plot into a shrine, a pilgrimage destination for
faithful to gather from “near and far.” App. 783–84. The shrine
would “honor Mary, the Mother of God, and would pay hom-
age to the sanctity of life.” Appellant’s Br. 16. With the help of
lawyers, architects, and traffic consultants, Holy Trinity de-
signed the shrine. It envisioned a 13,000-square-foot chapel
with gold domes, a bell tower, a museum, a gift shop, and a
retreat center.
 But the plot is constrained by Collier Township’s zoning
code. The code divides the township into districts, each of
which allows certain types of buildings. The northern, wooded
half of the plot lies in a planned-economic-development dis-
trict, allowing larger projects like business offices, amusement
parks, or country clubs. The southern half is in a rural-residen-
tial district, allowing farms and single-family homes. Neither
district contemplates shrines.

 2
  The zoning code is enforced by Collier’s five-member
Board of Commissioners. The Board has power not only to re-
zone land or amend the code, but also to approve or deny some
building projects, because the code makes some land uses con-
ditional. For instance, the code conditionally allows new
churches in rural-residential districts, but only if the Board ap-
proves them. In any event, anything as big as Holy Trinity’s
shrine needs the Board’s approval.
 To fit the shrine project into the zoning code, Holy Trinity
applied to do two things. First, it asked the Board to amend the
zoning code to allow planned cultural centers, including the
shrine, in economic-development districts. Second, it sought
to rezone some of its rural-residential land into economic-
development land, to make a larger plot for the shrine. As part
of its application, Holy Trinity included sketches of its shrine
plus a traffic study showing minimal impact on the surrounding
community. After a live hearing with concerned residents, the
Board denied Holy Trinity’s application, expressing concern
about traffic and Holy Trinity’s fundraising projections. Some
residents, and at least one Board member, were also troubled
once they learned that the shrine’s message would be pro-life.
 So Holy Trinity tried again with a smaller project. It applied
to build a modest chapel entirely on its rural-residential land.
Though the Board approved the new application, it came with
strings attached, limiting bell ringing, the height of the chapel,
and who could be remembered at memorial services. At first,
Holy Trinity appealed in state court, but then it abandoned that
appeal to file this federal lawsuit. It claims that the township’s
zoning code facially violates the First Amendment’s Free Exer-
cise Clause and the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized

 3
 Persons Act (RLUIPA), and that the denial of its initial rezon-
ing application violated those laws.
 Holy Trinity moved for a preliminary injunction. But the
District Court denied it, finding that Holy Trinity was not sub-
stantially likely to succeed on the merits, was unclear about
what relief it sought, and was seeking to change the status quo.
In sum, it explained, no injunction was needed to keep the case
alive.
 We have jurisdiction to review the denial of a preliminary
injunction under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1). We review the District
Court’s legal rulings de novo, its findings of fact for clear error,
and its ultimate decision for abuse of discretion. Del. State
Sportsmen’s Ass’n, Inc. v. Del. Dep’t of Safety & Homeland
Sec., 108 F.4th 194, 198 (3d Cir. 2024). We review “deferen-
tially” because “the denial of a preliminary injunction is almost
always based on an abbreviated set of facts, requiring a delicate
balancing that is the responsibility of the district judge.” Id.
(internal quotation marks omitted). And in seeking to overturn
a denial, Holy Trinity “bears a heavy burden.” Chesimard v.
Mulcahy, 570 F.2d 1184, 1187 (3d Cir. 1978).
 II. THE DISTRICT COURT PROPERLY PRESERVED
 THE STATUS QUO

 The parties here, like most parties disputing preliminary
injunctions, devote almost their entire briefs to the merits—as
if they are leaping to final judgment. That is a common error.
The “purpose of a preliminary injunction” is not to leapfrog
over trial and final judgment to the court of appeals, but
“merely to preserve the relative positions of the parties until a
trial on the merits can be held.” Univ. of Tex. v. Camenisch, 451

 4
 U.S. 390, 395 (1981). The main reason to grant this “extraor-
dinary remedy” is “to preserve the court’s power to render a
meaningful decision after a trial on the merits.” Del. State
Sportsmen’s, 108 F.4th at 201 (internal quotation marks
omitted).
 In exercising its discretion to grant a preliminary injunc-
tion, a trial court does look to the likelihood of success on the
merits. But it also weighs the risk of irreparable injury absent
preliminary relief, the balance of equities, and the public inter-
est. Winter v. NRDC, 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). When the govern-
ment is the defendant, the last two factors merge. Nken v.
Holder, 556 U.S. 418, 435 (2009). The moving party bears the
burden of persuading the trial court “by a clear showing.” Ma-
zurek v. Armstrong, 520 U.S. 968, 972 (1997) (per curiam)
(cleaned up). Holy Trinity’s burden is especially heavy because
it seeks to disrupt the status quo, putting its land to a new use.
See Ams. for Prosperity Found. v. Albence, 2026 WL 2563151,
at *2–3, ___ F.4th ___, ___ (3d Cir. 2026). It has not borne it.
 A. At trial, Holy Trinity is likely to win some relief
 Holy Trinity rightly argues that it is likely to win on at least
one of its claims. The township would have us believe that
Holy Trinity need only reapply to get its shrine—no harm, no
foul. But the record strongly suggests that the township is hos-
tile to the shrine project. If so, reapplying would be futile, and
Holy Trinity’s right to build a shrine is substantially burdened.
 RLUIPA specifically protects the right to “use, build[ ], or
conver[t]” “real property for the purpose of religious exercise.”
42 U.S.C. § 2000cc-5(7)(B). The township may not invoke its
zoning code “in a manner that imposes a substantial burden”

 5
 on Holy Trinity’s right to build unless it can show that doing
so is the least restrictive way to further a compelling interest.
§ 2000cc(a)(1).
 So we ask whether the burden on Holy Trinity is substan-
tial. Substantiality is “a question of degree.” Anash, Inc. v. Bor-
ough of Kingston, 184 F.4th 214, 239 (3d Cir. 2026). At one
end of the spectrum, the burden would be substantial if Holy
Trinity were kicked off its land or barred from ever building its
shrine. See id. at 240. (Anash’s facts were that extreme: The
town there had effectively evicted an existing congregation. Id.
at 246.) But merely having to jump through hoops, like reapply-
ing for rezoning, might not count on its own. Westchester Day
Sch. v. Vill. of Mamaroneck, 504 F.3d 338, 349 (2d Cir. 2007).
Indeed, Holy Trinity conceded as much at oral argument. If the
parish can clear that hurdle “quickly or easily,” it is hard to
view the burden as substantial. Anash, 184 F.4th at 240. But if
reapplying is futile, then the Board’s denial is tantamount to
barring the project.
 We think Holy Trinity is likely to show that the township’s
rejection effectively bars the project and thus substantially bur-
dens its chosen land use. First, although Holy Trinity was just
taking the first step of seeking rezoning (to be followed by
project-specific applications), the Board focused on the ulti-
mate shrine project. Second, residents overwhelmingly disap-
proved of the shrine project, not just the rezoning application.
 Finally, and most troubling, both community and Board
members objected to the shrine’s pro-life message. One resi-
dent worried that “Father Jason has been very involved in pro
life. This is to be a pro life museum … [W]hen you think very

 6
 political rights, either side, it brings a lot of danger, a lot of
protests, as well as costs that could be incurred by the commu-
nity.” App. 820. Another complained that “the intent of the
shrine was a celebration for Roe vs. Wade being overturned …
[and] reparation for sin of abortion and counseling, spiritual
direction …. this will bring a bunch [of people] potentially for
a rally and this could also bring the opposite as well for pro-
test.” App. 825–26.
 Privately, at least one of the Board’s members agreed. The
day after the hearing, that commissioner forwarded an email
about the shrine’s pro-life stance to the rest of the Board:
“Looks like we might have dodged a bullet last night. The true
inten[t] of the shrine” was pro-life and “This could have been a
disaster.” App. 874. Another township officer, copied on the
email, seemed to affirm those sentiments. Nothing in the record
suggests that any other Board member responded and disagreed.
And in her deposition, the Board member who wrote the email
confirmed that “one of the reasons” that the Board had denied
the application was Holy Trinity’s pro-life purpose. App. 215.
She also defended denying land-use approval “based on the na-
ture of the religious service to be held in the building.” App.
227.
 These objections hint at unconstitutional religious hostility
and content-based discrimination, concerns that would be bet-
ter addressed on a more developed factual record. Masterpiece
Cakeshop v. Colo. Civil Rights Comm’n, 584 U.S. 617, 638
(2018); Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155, 163–64 (2015).
But at the very least, they strongly suggest that the Board resists
ever approving the shrine project. If so, the rezoning denial is
effectively absolute, and the “degree” of burden on Holy

 7
 Trinity is substantial. Anash, 184 F.4th at 239. Plus, the town-
ship does not show that denying approval altogether is the
least-restrictive means to serve a compelling interest. That is
enough to show that Holy Trinity is very likely to prevail on its
RLUIPA substantial-burden claim.
 B. But the balance of equities favors the status quo
 Preliminary relief does not automatically follow whenever
a party is likely to win on the merits. That is because the “goal
